## Statement

Let $Y$ be any closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold, with two actual pointed Heegaard diagrams and specified complete compression-disk systems as in the closed-manifold definition. Assume Countable Choice. Up to orientation-preserving ambient transports of the diagrams, their marked points may be identified with one point $z$. Each diagram can then be equipped with an auxiliary oriented unknot $K$ and a second point $w$ so that $K$ crosses its splitting surface exactly at $w,z$, each half is a neat trivial arc disjoint from its compression disks, and it has explicit simultaneous bridge witnesses. After further ambient transports fixing $z$, both diagrams have the SAME auxiliary $K,w,z$.

There exist Morse function and descending-field endpoints on $Y$ realizing the two transported diagrams up to attaching-curve isotopies avoiding both marks. Each endpoint has one minimum and one maximum on $K$, its remaining critical points have indices one and two on the respective sides of the middle level, and the two endpoints agree with one fixed function and field germ on a common tube about $K$. All other critical points and the actual lower stable and upper unstable compression systems are retained through the final common-germ modification. No hypothesis on the homology or fundamental group of $Y$ is imposed. This is auxiliary geometric data, not an analytic basepoint insertion or a comparison of Floer complexes.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The input handlebodies are smooth regular neighborhoods of finite connected graphs, with actual complete compression disks and one basepoint off their boundaries. ([[def-hat-heegaard-floer-complex-of-a-closed-three-manifold]])

[F2] In a handlebody embedded in $S^3$, broad proper compression disks with ball cuts admit same-boundary neat replacements and actual standard smooth rounded cut balls. The replacement is supported in arbitrarily small disk-boundary collars and may avoid specified disjoint compact data. ([[lem-proper-compression-disks-admit-neat-witnesses-with-standard-cut-balls]])

[F3] Actual neat ball, compression and bridge data give adapted Morse endpoints on any compact oriented three-manifold with boundary. Their prescribed disks are tracked by the relative one-handle cocore comparisons. One-sided endpoints glue across a surface in any closed oriented three-manifold, changing attaching curves only by marked isotopies. Already adapted endpoints tangent to one marked circle admit a common protected germ on any such manifold. ([[lem-neatly-bridged-compression-data-admit-adapted-morse-endpoints]], [[lem-neat-marked-morse-endpoints-glue-across-a-heegaard-surface]], [[lem-adapted-knot-morse-endpoints-admit-a-common-protected-germ]])

[F4] A smooth auxiliary Riemannian metric exists under Countable Choice. Parameterized Euclidean local inverses, compactly supported smooth flows on a compact time interval and finite compact-set cutoffs are available. ([[cor-every-smooth-manifold-admits-a-riemannian-metric]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]], [[thm-compactly-supported-time-dependent-vector-fields-have-global-evolution-on-a-compact-time-interval]], [[lem-manifold-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]])

[A1] Only Countable Choice is assumed. All chart, graph, collar and handle selections added below are finite. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** The data and Countable Choice in the Statement.

1.1 Move distinct basepoints to a common point if necessary. In a connected manifold any two points are joined by a finite chain of coordinate balls: the points reachable by such a chain form an open set whose complement is also open. Inside each ball join successive centers by a smooth coordinate path with compact interior track. A smooth time-dependent field equal to its velocity on a small neighborhood of the moving point, extended by a cutoff, transports that point by its flow. A finite composition gives an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying one basepoint to the other. Transport its whole diagram, compression disks and splitting at the same time. This is an allowed embedded-diagram isomorphism, not a claim that its analytic action is the identity. Henceforth both basepoints are $z$. [F1, F4, A1, given, construct]

2.1 In a positive coordinate ball at $z$ straighten the splitting surface to $x_3=0$ and label its lower side $x_3<0$. Choose the ball disjoint from the entire finite compression-disk family: the disks are compact and none contains $z$, since their boundaries avoid it and their interiors are interior to their respective handlebodies. For sufficiently small $r>0$ put $$K_r(\theta)=(r(1-\cos\theta),0,r\sin\theta),\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.$$ Its two surface crossings are $z$ and $w=(2r,0,0)$ and are transverse. Its lower arc is oriented $w\to z$ and its upper arc $z\to w$. The two planar half-disks between its semicircles and the interval $[z,w]$ are explicit smooth corner bridge witnesses, neat at the surface edge. They miss all compression disks because their entire coordinate ball does. Each half arc belongs to the sole cut ball of its side. The full circle bounds the displayed planar disk in the ball, so it is an auxiliary local unknot with no global knot-type assertion needed. [F1, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The local round models from two positive charts based at the SAME $z$ are ambient isotopic fixing $z$, with their ordered $w,z$ and oriented circles carried along. Here are the germ and support details. Shrinking $r$ through positive radii gives an isotopy of the circle fixing $z$; a radial vector field, cut off outside a larger coordinate ball, extends it. For two coordinate germs fixing zero the transition $h$ is positive and smooth. The germs $h_a(x)=a^{-1}h(ax)$ extend smoothly at $a=0$ to $Dh(0)x$, by the integral formula $h_a(x)=\int_0^1Dh(sa x)x\,ds$. They are local diffeomorphisms on one uniform smaller ball, because their derivatives are uniformly close to the invertible $Dh(0)$. A positive matrix has a path to the identity: Gram–Schmidt gives a positive upper triangular factor, joined to its positive diagonal and then to the identity by straight interpolation; its orthogonal factor lies in $SO(3)$ and is a finite product of plane rotations. Thus the transition germ is joined to the identity through positive germs fixing zero. The velocity $\partial_a h_a\circ h_a^{-1}$ vanishes at zero. Extend it by a cutoff equal to one on the compact track of a sufficiently small model circle and zero outside the coordinate ball. The resulting flow fixes zero and agrees with the germ path on that track by uniqueness. Combine the shrinkings, this germ extension and inverse shrinkings. This carries one marked oriented local circle to the other while fixing $z$; $w$ is carried as its labelled other marked point. Carry each entire diagram and its disk and bridge data by this ambient map. We now have one actual $K,w,z$ for both endpoints. No simultaneous transport is said to preserve the old surface pointwise. [F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Prepare compression witnesses without assuming $Y$ embeds in $S^3$. Each handlebody is a smooth regular neighborhood of a finite graph. A spanning tree of that graph has a standard smooth ball neighborhood, obtained by repeatedly absorbing a leaf ball and its joining tube through disk collars. Every edge outside the tree supplies one framed one-handle. Conversely attaching these finitely many handles to a ball gives a smooth parametrization of the original regular neighborhood, by the same product edge and vertex charts. A ball with these finitely many handles has a standard embedding in $\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$: use disjoint small foot disks and disjoint arches, at distinct heights, for the remaining edges. Thus the abstract handlebody, independently of its embedding in $Y$, has a smooth parametrization into this standard model. Transport its actual auxiliary disks there, apply [F2], and pull the replacements and smooth cut-ball parameters back. This application is within $S^3$ only for the auxiliary model; it makes no Schoenflies assertion about a sphere in $Y$. Its supports may miss the local bridge witnesses, since those witnesses and disks were already disjoint in the local round-circle construction and remain disjoint after its ambient alignment. All attaching curves, actual arcs and surface marks are retained. The supplied complete system still cuts into ONE smoothly parametrized ball. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Apply [F3]'s one-sided construction to each actual cut ball with its single auxiliary arc, its explicit neat bridge half-disk and its transported face collars. It gives one lower minimum, the prescribed number of lower index-one points and their actual stable compression disks; the upper construction is dual. Glue them across the splitting by [F3]. The one-sided collar transports fix the surface, and the subsequent field interpolation changes the curves by its finite-time collar holonomy isotopies fixing $w,z$. Thus the endpoint diagram is the original transported diagram up to those allowed curve isotopies. Choose the ordinary critical heights distinct by the one-at-a-time finite handle order. There is no same-index trajectory: a lower index-one stable disk reaches the middle level as a compact disk and cannot terminate backwards at another index-one point; the upper assertion is dual. Index increase is excluded by the separated lower/upper groups and the empty outgoing or incoming spheres for extrema. [F3, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Choose the auxiliary smooth metric by [F4] and use the common-germ clause of [F3] on the two resulting pairs, with the SAME actual oriented $K,w,z$ from the local-model alignment. Its ambient maps preserve $K$ and fix the marks. Transport the surfaces and disk systems too. At the final field blend choose its common tube smaller than the distance to BOTH finite compact transported lower stable and upper unstable disk systems. These systems are disjoint from $K$: its trajectories end at the protected extrema. The blend is therefore absent on every one of those actual systems and on all other critical charts. Each retained invariant disk still has its original local critical model; uniqueness of trajectories proves it is still the full truncated stable or unstable disk. No endpoint same-index trajectory has been introduced. The endpoint functions and fields now agree near $K$, with exactly one protected minimum and maximum and no other tube critical point. Every endpoint change has been an explicit allowed ambient transport or a marked curve isotopy. All auxiliary objects can be forgotten after a geometric comparison; no chain-map assertion has been made. [F3, F4, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Take the grid on $\mathbb R^2/(5\mathbb Z)^2$ with marks $O_r=(r+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ and $X_r=((r+2)\bmod5+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ for $0\le r<5$. Let $C$ have the $120$ grid states as its $\mathbb F_2$-basis, Maslov grading $M_{\mathbb O}$ and Alexander filtration $A_G$. Its differential counts empty directed torus rectangles avoiding every $O$ but allowing $X$; equivalently, it is the full filtered minus matrix with all five variables set to zero. Then $C$ is a filtered chain complex and is filtered chain homotopy equivalent, preserving Maslov grading, to $S\otimes V^{\otimes4}$. Here $S$ has basis $a,b,c$ at respective $(M,A)$ values $(0,-1),(1,0),(2,1)$ with $\partial c=b$ and other differential zero, and $V$ has zero differential and basis at $(M,A)=(0,0),(-1,-1)$.

In particular, $H(C)$ has rank $16$. Its homology classes in Maslov degree $-k$, $0\le k\le4$, have multiplicity $\binom4k$ and first appear in Alexander filtration $-1-k$. This is a calculation of the specified grid matrix; no knot type or normalized analytic knot Floer identification is asserted.

## Statement references

[[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Exactly the grid, directed-rectangle matrix and gradings in the Statement, over $\mathbb F_2$.

[F1] The grid definition [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] specifies southwest/northeast source corners and the pair-count formulas for $M_{\mathbb O},M_{\mathbb X},A_G$.

[F2] The full filtered mode of [[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex]] allows $X$ and weights each $O$ by its own variable; setting every variable to zero retains exactly the $O$-free rectangles.

## Proof

1.1 Index states by $0,\ldots,119$ in lexicographic order of permutations $p=(p_0,\ldots,p_4)$, representing points $(p_r,r)$. For distinct $r,s$, the candidate rectangle starts southwest at $(p_r,r)$ and ends northeast at $(p_s,s)$, using positive cyclic coordinate intervals. Put $\delta(u,v)=(v-u)\bmod5$ and say $z$ is inside that interval if $0<\delta(u,z)<\delta(u,v)$. Keep the candidate precisely when no state point and no $O$ point satisfies both interior tests; its target is obtained by swapping $p_r,p_s$. Add targets by symmetric difference. This enumerates both directed rectangles for each transposition and exactly realizes [F1]–[F2]. The finite matrix given by this recipe has $D^2p=0$ at each of its120 columns; direct multiplication is reproduced by the exact finite certificate below. Each retained term has $M$ decrease one and nonnegative $A$ decrease, checked in the same enumeration from the pair-count formulas. Thus $C$ is a filtered chain complex. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 An arrow $u\mapsto v+z$ with coefficient one and $A(u)=A(v)$ may be cancelled by replacing each other differential column $D(w)$ by $D(w)+[v]D(w)D(u)$, then deleting rows and columns $u,v$; here $[v]D(w)$ is the coefficient of $v$. To verify the equivalence, first replace the basis vector $v$ by $D(u)=v+z$, then replace each other generator $w$ by $w+[v]D(w)u$. The chain identity $D^2=0$ makes the two-dimensional span of $u,D(u)$ an independent contractible summand. Every change preserves the filtration: all terms of $z$ have level at most $A(v)=A(u)$, and whenever $v$ occurs in $D(w)$ one has $A(w)\ge A(v)$. The changes also preserve Maslov grading. Contract that summand by $D(u)\mapsto u$, which preserves filtration because the two levels agree. Applying the36 pivots in the certificate yields a filtered homotopy equivalent48-generator matrix. The displayed reduced columns and equal-level pivot recurrence permit direct verification of every entry. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 In that reduced matrix every generator satisfies $A=M-1$. For $M=-4,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2$, the chain dimensions are respectively $1,5,11,14,11,5,1$, and the outgoing differential ranks are $0,0,1,4,6,4,1$. The certificate gives independent image columns and expresses every other nonzero column in them. Rank-nullity therefore gives homology multiplicities $1,4,6,4,1,0,0$ at those respective degrees. In each degree choose a basis for boundaries, extend to a basis of cycles, and extend once more to all chains. The differential identifies the last complement with boundaries one degree lower. Since every vector in a fixed Maslov degree has the same Alexander level $M-1$, these changes of basis preserve filtration. Thus the reduced complex splits as its homology generators and two-term pairs. There are $\binom4k$ homology generators at $(M,A)=(-k,-1-k)$ and $\binom4k$ pairs whose source has $(M,A)=(2-k,1-k)$ and target $(1-k,-k)$, for $0\le k\le4$. These are precisely the homology generators and pairs of $S\otimes V^{\otimes4}$; matching bases gives the stated filtered isomorphism after cancellation. The birth levels follow because all homology representatives in a degree have its specified single Alexander level. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the actual marked Seifert surface of genus g, oriented as minus the fiber for the cut, an adapted generator x has Alexander degree g minus the number of its interior polygon coordinates. Thus the top degree-g generators are exactly the outer generators and correspond to the cut diagram generators with their ordered intersection signs. If the integral top homology is one copy of the integers, the actual cut incidence matrix is unimodular, the cut is an integral homology product, and its periodic-domain group vanishes.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-integral-sutured-floer-compactness-and-orientations]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F2] [[lem-marked-fiber-admits-a-sutured-surface-diagram]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F3] [[def-top-alexander-grading-of-knot-floer-homology]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F4] [[def-sutured-floer-chain-complex]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F5] [[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

## Proof

**Given:** The actual diagrams, markings, orientation classes, and admissibility hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 The actual binding bridge and drilled diagram carry the oriented Seifert surface and its page framing. Set S=−F, with the orientation used for the sutured cut. Use the meridional boundary trivialization t_μ from the Alexander definition, not a trivialization transported from an unmarked closed diagram. [construct]

1.2 **The relative Euler obstruction.** Represent a generator's relative Spin^c structure by its Morse vector field with the selected index-one/index-two trajectories removed and locally replaced by the standard nonvanishing fields. On S project its orthogonal plane field to TS away from these local trajectory patches. Its relative Euler obstruction is the sum of three contributions: the tangent Euler number χ(S); the half-index at each crossing of ∂S with a suture; and the rotation correction of the specified boundary trivialization. A crossing contributes −1/2: in the oriented sutured collar the positive and negative normal fields are joined by a half-turn opposite the positive tangent boundary rotation. The two meridional crossings therefore give I(S)=−1. The page longitude and the actual meridional collar frame have zero extra rotation relative to one another, so r(S,t_μ)=0. This uses the actual fiber marking; a different longitude framing would change this term. [construct]

1.3 For an outer field no selected trajectory pierces the interior of S. Hence its obstruction is χ(S)+I(S)−r(S,t_μ)=(1−2g)−1=−2g. At an interior coordinate of the adapted polygon, the Morse replacement has the local model of a trajectory piercing S once. The orthogonal two-plane frame on the boundary of that small patch turns twice positively relative to the outer model: one turn from each side of the removed trajectory tube. Its relative obstruction therefore increases by two. The patches are disjoint and all other local frames agree. If n_P(x) counts the generator coordinates in the polygon interior, additivity of the relative Euler obstruction gives [construct]

1.4 ⟨c₁(s(x),t_μ),[−F]⟩ = −2g+2n_P(x), A_F(x) = ½⟨c₁(s(x),t_μ),[F]⟩ = g−n_P(x). [construct]

1.5 Thus no generator has Alexander degree greater than g, and its degree is g exactly when it is outer. The local sign is fixed by orienting S=−F and by the carried page longitude; reversing S reverses the Chern evaluation. This proves the absolute anchor, not merely a relative difference of Alexander gradings. [construct]

1.6 **The actual cut generator set.** In the cut/double surface diagram, a generator cannot enter the forbidden copy of P: the α and β boundary conditions occupy its opposite copies. Every generator is therefore the unique lift of an outer generator, and every outer generator lifts. This correspondence preserves the ordered α/β intersection signs, since each intersection neighborhood is copied with its surface orientation. Consequently the Euler sum of the top Alexander module is exactly the signed intersection sum of the cut diagram. This is the generator-level identification used in the integral matrix reduction before asserting a signed differential comparison. [construct]

2.1 Research donor for the Ni original, 2026-10-20. This proves the homology-product operation once the actual signed sutured complex has been constructed. It supplies neither that construction nor the product-detection theorem. [construct]

2.2 **Claim with exact inputs.** Assume Countable Choice as used by the general real-strip Fredholm supplier. Let $(\Sigma,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta)$ be an actual finite transverse balanced sutured diagram for a connected oriented compact three-manifold $M$. Suppose its compressed lower and upper surfaces $R_-$ and $R_+$ are connected. There are $d$ curves in each family, and both compressed surfaces have nonempty boundary. Supply the actual finite integral disk-count complex $C$, with differential squaring to zero and counting index-one Whitney strips. No absolute Maslov grading, rational-homology-sphere hypothesis, or three-sphere comparison is assumed. [construct]

2.3 If the total integral homology of this supplied complex is $\mathbb Z$, then [construct]

2.4 $$H_*(M,R_-;\mathbb Z)=H_*(M,R_+;\mathbb Z)=0.$$ [construct]

2.5 Thus $M$ is an integral homology product. The conclusion is weaker than being a product sutured manifold and does not imply fiberedness by itself. [construct]

2.6 **1. The exact relative handle matrix.** Orient and order the attaching curves. Set $I_{ij}=\alpha_i\cdot\beta_j$, using the oriented surface intersection number. Compressing $\Sigma$ along all alpha curves gives $R_-$. In the diagram's handle description the lower compression body is obtained by attaching two-handles to $\Sigma\times[-1,0]$ at the lower end. Reverse this description: it is $R_-\times[0,1]$ with $d$ one-handles. The alpha circles on its upper boundary are precisely their belt circles. There are no additional zero-handles: the compressed surface is the connected nonempty $R_-$, and no closed compressed component is present in a balanced diagram. The upper beta compressions attach $d$ two-handles. They give the diagram-defined $M$; by the same balance condition no sphere or other closed compressed component requires a three-handle. [construct]

2.7 The relative cellular handle complex for $(M,R_-)$ is therefore [construct]

2.8 $$0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^d\xrightarrow{\ I\ }\mathbb Z^d\longrightarrow0,$$ [construct]

2.9 in degrees two and one. To verify the matrix, push each attaching beta circle slightly into the boundary transverse to the one-handle belt circles. An oriented traversal through the $i$th one-handle contributes $+1$ or $-1$ according to its crossing of the oriented belt circle $\alpha_i$. Collapsing the one-handle cores to their relative one-cells reads exactly this sum as the degree of the beta attaching circle on that cell. Thus its $i,j$ incidence number is $\alpha_i\cdot\beta_j$, after choosing the corresponding core orientations. Changing one handle orientation multiplies its row or column by $-1$, which has no effect on unimodularity. This is the actual relative handle complex, not a closed-manifold $H_1(Y)$ presentation. [construct]

2.10 Applying the reversed construction from $R_+$ gives the transpose matrix up to row and column signs, with the surface orientation reversed if necessary. Consequently it is enough to prove $\det I=\pm1$. [construct]

2.11 **2. A parity needing no three-sphere normalization.** For every generator $\mathbf x$ let $\sigma_{\mathbf x}$ be the permutation matching its ordered alpha labels to its ordered beta labels, and put [construct]

2.12 $$q(\mathbf x)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma_{\mathbf x})\prod_{i=1}^d\operatorname{sgn}_{\Sigma}(\alpha_i',\beta_{\sigma_{\mathbf x}(i)}')(x_i).$$ [construct]

2.13 This is a globally defined sign on all generators, including generators in different Spin-c classes. Expanding the determinant by permutations and expanding each algebraic intersection sum gives [construct]

2.14 $$\sum_{\mathbf x}q(\mathbf x)=\det I.$$ [construct]

2.15 The sign of the actual intersection of the ordered product tori is $\epsilon(\mathbf x)=c_dq(\mathbf x)$, with $c_d=(-1)^{d(d-1)/2}$. Indeed the tangent columns are the $d$ alpha vectors followed by the $d$ beta vectors. Reorder beta vectors to the matching alpha slots, giving $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma_{\mathbf x}$, and interleave the two blocks into their oriented surface-coordinate planes, giving $c_d$. The remaining two-dimensional determinants are exactly the local surface signs above. Symmetric coordinates add no real orientation sign, because a permutation of complex coordinate factors preserves real orientation. [construct]

2.16 For each Whitney strip actually counted in $C$, [construct]

2.17 $$(-1)^{\mu(\phi)}=\epsilon(\mathbf x)\epsilon(\mathbf y)=q(\mathbf x)q(\mathbf y).$$ [construct]

2.18 Here is precisely the general operator calculation used, without importing an $S^3$ grading statement. Orient the two pulled-back boundary bundles by their global ordered product-circle frames. The real-frame construction in `lem-geometric-strip-linearization-frame-and-fredholm-index`, steps 2.1--6.1, compares the two transported terminal boundary frames with the chosen terminal complex frame by signs $\sigma_0,\sigma_1$. It constructs $\ell=p-2k$, with $(-1)^p=\sigma_0\sigma_1$, and proves that the index of the actual strip operator is $-\ell$. Therefore its index parity is $\sigma_0\sigma_1$. At the two endpoints the complex changes of coordinates have positive real determinant; the remaining real basis comparison is exactly the ratio of the ordered-torus intersection signs. Thus $\sigma_0\sigma_1=\epsilon(\mathbf x)\epsilon(\mathbf y)$, proving the formula. One may choose the actual product-integrable endpoint charts furnished by that supplier so its exact end hypothesis applies. No generator-to-generator Whitney class is required when no such class occurs, no equality of Spin-c labels is needed across unrelated generators, and no absolute even/odd origin is chosen by total $\widehat{HF}(S^3)$. 2.19 Every counted differential strip has index one, so the differential reverses $q$. Regard $C$ as a finite parity complex, even for $q=+1$ and odd for $q=-1$. Its Euler characteristic is consequently $\det I$. [construct]

2.20 **3. Unimodularity and integral acyclicity.** Tensor $C$ with $\mathbb Q$. Tensoring by this localization is exact, so its total homology is $\mathbb Q$ by the supplied integral homology hypothesis. Its two parity homologies form a direct sum with total dimension one; one has dimension one and the other zero. Hence its Euler characteristic is $+1$ or $-1$. [construct]

2.21 For completeness the equality of Euler characteristics of this finite parity complex and its homology uses only rank-nullity. Its reversed counterpart from $R_+$ is acyclic as well. These complexes compute the two asserted relative homology groups, completing the claim. ## Statement

Let $G$ be a finite nonempty planar marked grid with vertical-over crossing convention. A horizontal segment is a cap if its two incident vertical segments both extend above it or both extend below it; otherwise it is monotone. A marked stabilization splits a marked cell into a two-by-two block with the chosen marking type twice at opposite corners, the other type once and one empty corner, preserving one of each type per row and column. A legal column commutation exchanges adjacent columns with disjoint or strictly nested closed vertical marking intervals. There is a finite sequence of marked stabilizations and legal commutations carrying $G$ to a grid in which every cap has no crossing and every monotone horizontal segment has exactly one crossing. Thus the resulting grid is bridge-like: slightly tilt its crossing-containing horizontal segments in the direction of height travel and round its empty caps to obtain a bridge diagram. Every operation respects the oriented $O,X$ convention of the grid-diagram definition, and the number of link components is unchanged. The decorated planar diagram before and after the entire refinement is planar isotopic after rounding corners; in particular no Reidemeister move is needed for this refinement. No global grid-move generation theorem is assumed.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite nonempty marked grid. Every row and column has one mark of each type, and all horizontal and vertical coordinates are distinct.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] fixes the marking and vertical-over convention.

## Proof

1.1 We first describe a row-splitting operation with full marking data. Write the chosen row as $H$, its left endpoint column as $A$, its right endpoint column as $B$, and its marks there as $a,b$, respectively, where $\{a,b\}=\{O,X\}$. Insert a new row $H'$ immediately above or immediately below $H$, and a column $C$ immediately to the right of $A$. Replace the $a$ at $(A,H)$ by $$a\text{ at }(A,H'),\qquad b\text{ at }(C,H'),\qquad a\text{ at }(C,H).$$ Keep the $b$ at $(B,H)$. If $H'>H$, the new block has $a$ northwest and southeast, $b$ northeast and empty southwest; if $H'<H$, it has $a$ southwest and northeast, $b$ southeast and empty northwest. Both are allowed stabilizations. Each new row and column has one mark of each type, and the old column $A$ retains its complementary exterior mark. The oriented path is obtained by subdividing the same old row path into a horizontal, vertical, horizontal path; its incidence with the rest of the link is unchanged. [F1, given, construct, cases]

2.1 The new column $C$ has closed vertical interval between the consecutive levels $H,H'$. An old column strictly between $A,B$ has no endpoint at $H$, since the only old endpoints there are $A,B$; it has no endpoint at the newly inserted $H'$. Since no old row lies between $H,H'$, that old column's interval either contains $[H,H']$ in its interior or is disjoint from it. Thus $C$ can be commuted to any specified column gap strictly between $A,B$, one adjacent old column at a time, by legal commutations. Stop before $B$. The resulting path replacing the old row is $A$ at height $H'$, horizontally to $C$, vertically to height $H$, and horizontally to $B$. At an old column strictly between $A,B$, its vertical segment crosses height $H'$ if and only if it crosses $H$, because neither level is an endpoint and no old endpoint level lies between them. Hence the old crossings of row $H$ are divided, in their original order, between the two new horizontal segments, with no extra crossing. [F1, step 1.1, given, construct, cases]

3.1 No other horizontal row changes its crossing count or cap/monotone type. The short column $C$ meets no such level; changing the endpoint of column $A$ from $H$ to the adjacent $H'$ passes no other row; and each old column commuted with $C$ moves across no other old column. Thus its incidences and its order relative to all other old columns are unchanged. For an exterior row incident to a moved column, its endpoint moves only across the short new column, which has no intersection with that exterior row. For an exterior row incident to $A$, the direction of its vertical leg is unchanged since $H,H'$ are consecutive levels. These observations verify the claim for both kinds of exterior row, including rows whose horizontal intervals strictly contain the new short column. We additionally verify planar isotopy, not just crossing counts. Choose a band about $H$ containing no other old row, and choose $H'$ arbitrarily close to $H$ inside it. In a narrow column gap about the final position of $C$, replace the short vertical jog by a steep smooth graph connecting the heights $H'$ and $H$; the gap contains no old column. The replacement of the old row is now a smooth graph $y=f(x)$, equal to $H'$ on the left and $H$ on the right outside that gap. For every $x$ choose an increasing smooth vertical reparameterization supported in the row band that sends $H$ to $f(x)$. Such reparameterizations exist smoothly in $x$: take a fixed bump equal to one near the two close heights and use $y\mapsto y+(f(x)-H)\chi(y)$, choosing $|H'-H|\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$. Interpolating its displacement with zero gives a plane isotopy. It keeps every old vertical line setwise, carries its intersection with the old row to the correct new height, and changes no exterior horizontal row. At the two endpoint columns it carries the incident vertical endpoint to the prescribed new endpoint. Rounding the steep connecting graph into the new vertical jog inside its empty gap is an isotopy of that embedded arc fixing its endpoints; use the same monotone graph interpolation before rounding. Thus the new decorated diagram is planar isotopic to the old one, with all crossing decorations fixed. The short-column commutations only select this empty gap and do not change any old-column order, so this proof covers their whole composite. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, cases]

3.2 Let $s_A,s_B\in\{+1,-1\}$ record whether the other endpoint of column $A$, respectively $B$, is above or below $H$. These signs are also the directions of those old vertical legs relative to the adjacent new levels. Put $\epsilon=\operatorname{sign}(H'-H)$. At the new horizontal segment $A$--$C$ in row $H'$, the two vertical-leg signs are $s_A,-\epsilon$. At the retained segment $C$--$B$ in row $H$, they are $\epsilon,s_B$. These formulas give all the following cases without a pictorial assumption. If the old row is a cap, $s_A=s_B=s$, choose $\epsilon=-s$ and leave $C$ in the immediate gap after $A$. The new $H'$ segment is a cap with zero crossings, and the retained $H$ segment is monotone with all the old crossings. If the old row is monotone, $s_A=-s_B$, choose $\epsilon=s_A$ to make both new segments monotone; choose instead $\epsilon=s_B$ to make both new segments caps. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra, cases]

4.1 Apply the splitting rule to a bad row as follows. A cap with $k\ge1$ crossings is treated by the first case of step 3.2, producing one empty cap and one monotone row with $k$ crossings. A monotone row with zero crossings is treated by its second sign choice in step 3.2, producing two empty caps. A monotone row with $k\ge2$ crossings is treated by its first sign choice; commute $C$ to a gap after the first crossing and before the second. Such a gap exists because distinct crossing columns are distinct and strictly between $A,B$. The two resulting monotone rows then have one and $k-1$ crossings. A cap with zero crossings or a monotone row with one crossing needs no operation. All choices are finite and allow either orientation through the variable $a$. [step 2.1, step 3.2, construct, cases]

5.1 Define a nonnegative integer on grids by summing, over all rows, the following contribution: for a cap with $k$ crossings use $k$; for a monotone row with $k\ge1$ crossings use $k-1$; for a monotone row with zero crossings use $1$. In the three bad cases of step 4.1 the total contribution changes respectively from $k$ to $k-1$, from $1$ to $0$, and from $k-1$ to $k-2$. Every other row's contribution is unchanged by step 3.1. Thus each operation reduces the integer by exactly one, and after finitely many operations it is zero. A zero contribution means precisely an empty cap or a one-crossing monotone row. Each operation was an actual marked stabilization followed by finitely many actual legal commutations. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Finally choose disjoint small horizontal bands about the row levels of the resulting grid. Tilt each monotone horizontal segment so that its traversal passes strictly monotonically from one incident vertical leg to the other; it has only one crossing, which remains a transverse vertical-over crossing. Round its two corners without a height extremum. Replace each empty cap by a smooth arch with precisely one nondegenerate height extremum in its band, rounding its corners into the incident vertical legs; its empty horizontal interval and a sufficiently thin band avoid every other strand. Distinct bands give distinct special heights, and the crossing preimages are not height-critical. Outside the bands the pieces are vertical. These changes are planar isotopies in small neighborhoods of the embedded edges and crossings, with their decorations fixed. This constructs the asserted smoothing. Because each marked row split only subdivided one oriented path and each column commutation transported the same incidence graph, none of the operations changes the number or orientation of components. This proves the claim by explicit finite moves. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Use oriented marked grids with vertical segments over horizontal ones. A stabilization splits one row and column through a chosen marking into a three-mark two-by-two block: the chosen type occurs twice at opposite corners, the other type once, and the last corner is empty; one mark of each type remains in every row and column. A commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns with disjoint or strictly nested closed marking intervals. In the patterns below $\bar a$ denotes the other type from $a\in\{O,X\}$, and all unspecified markings belong to an arbitrary valid exterior grid.

The following are marked grid certificates for R1, R2 and R3, respectively.

* R1: choose a corner $(P,H)$ of type $a$, its row partner $(B,H)$ of type $\bar a$ with $P<B$, and its column partner $(P,T)$ with $H<T$. Insert $C$ immediately left of $P$ and $H'$ immediately above $H$. Replace the old row marks by $(P,H,a),(C,H,\bar a),(C,H',a),(B,H',\bar a)$. This one stabilization inserts one Reidemeister kink, up to planar isotopy.
* R2: suppose $P,R$ are adjacent columns in that order, $K<H$ are consecutive rows, and the closed vertical interval of $P$ has endpoints $V<K<H<T$. Column $R$ has endpoints $K,H$. The row marks are $H:(A,a),(R,\bar a)$ and $K:(D,\bar a),(R,a)$, where $A,D<P$, the other endpoint of $A$ is above $H$, and that of $D$ is below $K$. Commuting $P,R$ removes the two crossings of $P$ with these rows and realizes R2.
* R3: suppose $P,R$ are adjacent columns in that order and $K<L<H$ are three consecutive rows. Column $P$ has endpoints $V<K<H<T$, and column $R$ has endpoints $K,H$. The row marks are $H:(A,a),(R,\bar a)$, $K:(R,a),(C,\bar a)$ and $L:(D,b),(E,\bar b)$, with $D<A<P<R<C<E$. The other endpoint of $A$ is above $H$, and that of $C$ is below $K$. Commuting $P,R$ realizes R3: the crossing between the top strand $P$ and the middle strand moves from row $H$ to row $K$, while the two crossings with the bottom strand in row $L$ change order.

In R2 and R3 the two types on column $P$ may be chosen in either order, subject to being part of the given grid. All indicated orientation choices, both directions of each move, and the horizontally and vertically reflected coordinate recipes are allowed. These models include every local sign/orientation variant of R1 and R2 and every consistent strict over/under height order and orientation variant of R3. The assertion is about these explicit finite models; a relative rectangularization placing an arbitrary surrounding diagram into their adjacency patterns is a separate obligation.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid finite marked grid satisfying one of the indicated patterns, with the specified local definitions of stabilization and commutation.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] supplies the row $O$-to-$X$, column $X$-to-$O$, and vertical-over conventions.

[F2] [[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]] includes both kink signs, all orientations of R1/R2, and all orientation variants of R3 with a consistent strict top/middle/bottom order; the cyclic over/under triangle is excluded.

## Proof

1.1 In R1 the stabilization block has north row $H'$, south row $H$, west column $C$, east column $P$. Its northwest and southeast corners have $a$, its southwest has $\bar a$, and its northeast is empty. The chosen original mark $a$ at $(P,H)$ is retained and duplicated at $(C,H')$; its old row partner moves from $(B,H)$ to $(B,H')$. Column $P$ keeps its exterior $\bar a$ at $T$, and column $B$ keeps its exterior $a$. Thus every new and retained row and column has exactly one mark of each type. This is a legitimate stabilization, including the relocated exterior row partner. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 In R2, $[K,H]$ is strictly contained in $[V,T]$. Therefore the adjacent-column exchange is legal. In the narrow vertical strip containing $P,R$, initially each row $H,K$ extends from a column left of $P$ to $R$, and so crosses $P$ once. Their pieces join through the vertical segment $R$; the other incoming leg at $A$ extends upward and the outgoing leg at $D$ downward. Thus these two rows and column $R$ form one strand making a horizontal excursion across $P$ and back, while $P$ is over at both crossings. After the exchange their endpoints at $R$ lie left of $P$, and both crossings disappear. There are no other horizontal levels between $K,H$, so the excursion bounds an empty bigon in this narrow strip. This is exactly the two-strand R2 removal. [F1, F2, given, construct]

1.3 In R3 the same strict interval containment makes the column exchange legal. Initially row $H$ runs from $A<P$ to $R$ and crosses $P$ once, while row $K$ runs from $R$ to $C$ and does not cross $P$. Row $L$ runs from $D$ to $E$ and crosses both $P,R$. It meets neither vertical leg at $A,C$, because the $A$ leg lies above $H$ and the $C$ leg below $K$. Hence in this strip there are exactly three crossings: $P$ over the middle strand in row $H$, $P$ over the bottom row $L$, and the middle vertical strand $R$ over that bottom row. After the exchange, row $H$ no longer crosses $P$, row $K$ does cross it, and the bottom row crosses the now reversed column order $R,P$. The three over/under relations are unchanged. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 The R1 model’s unoriented local path runs down $P$ from $T$ past level $H'$ to $H$, left to $C$, up to $H'$, and right past $P$ toward $B$. The new row at $H'$ crosses $P$ exactly once. The short return path through $C$ and row $H$ contains no other column or row level, so it encloses an otherwise empty small kink. Other old columns that crossed the original segment between $P,B$ also cross the slightly displaced segment at $H'$: their endpoint levels are not strictly between these consecutive levels. No other old row is crossed by moving the endpoint in column $B$. Consequently all exterior changes are planar displacements in an empty thin strip and preserve their crossings, while the neighborhood of $P,H$ undergoes precisely R1. If $a=O$, traversal down $P$ encounters the overpassing branch first; if $a=X$, traversal is reversed and the underpassing branch is encountered first. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, cases]

2.2 The two R2 crossings have opposite signs: along the excursion the two horizontal traversals have opposite horizontal directions, whereas the oriented direction of the vertical $P$ strand is fixed. Reversing either strand reverses both signs and preserves their opposition. The variable $a$ reverses the excursion orientation, and the two choices of top/bottom type in column $P$ reverse the other strand. These are the four independent orientation patterns. Exterior rows above $H$ or below $K$ do not meet the short column $R$; moving the adjacent long column $P$ across that absent short segment there changes no crossing. The endpoints of rows $H,K$ on other old columns do not move. Hence all other changes are planar displacements, with no extra local Reidemeister event. [F1, step 1.2, construct, cases]

2.3 These are the two sides of R3, not merely two diagrams with three crossings. In the narrow strip the top arc is $P$, the middle arc enters along $H$, turns down $R$, and exits along $K$, while the bottom arc passes straight across at $L$. The column exchange transfers the top-middle crossing from above the middle-bottom crossing to below it and interchanges their positions along the bottom arc. They bound the usual empty triangular region before and after the slide. There are no further horizontal levels between $K,H$ and no further vertical column between $P,R$. Thus its interior contains no other local strand or vertex. Any crossings of the long row portions outside this strip are unchanged, as are all exterior rows where $R$ is absent. This is exactly the R3 of [F2] with top $P$, middle $R$-excursion, and bottom row $L$. [F2, step 1.3, construct]

3.1 Every marking table in R3 extends both orientations of each of these three arcs independently whenever the exterior grid does: the choice of $a$ reverses the middle arc, the choice of $b$ reverses the bottom arc, and the type at the upper endpoint of $P$ reverses the top arc. The two marks on each of rows $H,K,L$ and on column $R$ remain complementary, so this is a marked certificate for all eight orientation patterns. An R3 crossing pattern has exactly one top, one middle and one bottom arc by [F2]; assigning them these roles treats every strict height order of the original named strands. The three pairwise crossing arcs have cyclically alternating endpoints on the local boundary. Up to cyclic starting point there are only the two opposite cyclic orders of their three names; the reflected recipe treats the other order. Thus no allowed height-order or local endpoint-order case is excluded. The cyclic over/under pattern would have no top arc and is not an R3 in [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.3, step 2.3, construct, cases]

4.1 Finally reflection of a whole coordinate recipe in either axis preserves adjacent levels, disjointness and strict containment of intervals, and takes an allowed three-mark stabilization block to another such block. It preserves vertical-over crossings. It gives recipes for the opposite local side and for a minimum in place of a maximum, without asserting that a grid is move-equivalent to its reflection. A single reflection reverses crossing signs, so the two kink signs in R1 and both sign orders in R2 are included. Together with the orientation reversals checked in steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1, this exhausts the variants specified in [F2]. Reversing each listed grid operation gives the reverse Reidemeister move. This proves exactly the finite pattern assertions; no claim about constructing their relative exterior fit has been used. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, construct, cases] ∎

3.4 No splitting of A+B in H, no nondegeneracy of the intersection form, and no omission of its radical is used. Similarly K₃≅C⊕B, with (u,v)↦(u,v,−u−v). The main pair periodic groups are C; the auxiliary pair groups are B. These are the full domain groups, not only a convenient subgroup. [construct]

3.5 For d≥2 all these domain relations are realized by polygon classes whenever the corner component is nonempty: the boundary loop in the symmetric product represents the sum of the displayed attaching-circle classes, and π₁(Sym^dΣ)=H₁Σ. The sum is zero, so it fills. Two fillings with the same domain differ by a zero-domain sphere; its complex determinant orientation is fixed. For d=0 there are no moving coordinates. For d=1, the already constructed actual boundary-region stabilization first gives d=2 by a literal integral chain isomorphism, so no abelianization assertion about Sym¹Σ is needed. [construct]

3.6 **A reference orientation and the character calculation.** Use the actual ordered global tangent frames of the attaching tori. Cut each polygon operator along its boundary and cap its framed real boundary segments. The closed complex part has its complex orientation; the ordered real caps and the translation/modulus factors have their specified order. A change of the cutting uses the same finite-kernel splice isomorphism as for strips. Its associativity follows by identifying both orders with the determinant of the same augmented kernel, with the same ordered cokernel columns. A periodic loop does not introduce an unrecorded frame sign: the tangent frames are global on the tori. The zero-domain sphere factor is complex oriented. This constructs a reference coherent orientation for this finite move configuration. It is not a choice of independently positive signs for its rigid polygons. [construct]

3.7 Relative to this reference, any other coherent orientation is a Z/2-character of the actual domain group, modulo generator orientation changes. Let h₀₁,h₁₂,h₀₂:B→Z/2 be the auxiliary pair characters. The already constructed auxiliary top-triangle unit fixes their compatibility as [construct]

3.8 h₀₂ = h₀₁+h₁₂. [construct]

3.9 Let m₀:C→Z/2 be the specified orientation class on (α,β). A triangle character on K₃ is of the form φ(u,v)=m(u)+h(v). Restricting it to the three pairs gives [construct]

3.10 (α,β): m(u)+h(u), (α,γ): m(u), (β,γ): h(v). [construct]

3.11 Thus, once the actual auxiliary unit class is fixed, the transported class on (α,γ) is forced to be [construct]

3.12 m₁ = m₀+h₀₁|C. [construct]

3.13 This is an affine transport relative to the specified reference; in particular it does not identify all characters of C. Apply it a second time to get m₂=m₁+h₁₂|C. A character on K₄ of the form q(u)+r(v)+s(w) restricts to [construct]

3.14 (α,β): q+r|C,     (α,γ): q+s|C,     (α,δ): q, (β,γ): r+s,       (γ,δ): s,          (β,δ): r. [construct]

3.15 Taking q=m₂, r=h₀₂ and s=h₁₂ realizes all six required pair classes simultaneously. This explicitly checks the stabilizer condition even when C≠0. It explains why prescribing the three exterior orientation systems independently would be wrong, and why transporting the specified one works. Every boundary-radical element of C is evaluated by the same formulas. [construct]

3.16 The same computation applies to each finite quadrilateral used for a slide, its inverse slide, and the small-isotopy comparison. Choose the classes successively along the move word and use this simultaneous extension on each inverse/composition configuration. At an end repeated diagram use the transported original class. A different move word need not induce the same automorphism; an isomorphism of the homology groups is what is needed here. [construct]

3.17 **Consequence for admitted actual multidiagrams.** On an actual weakly admissible configuration, the new signed exterior compactification and these compatible determinant orientations give the integer triangle and quadrilateral identities. The already constructed auxiliary unit and finite triangular isotopy inverse then give the signed handleslide equivalence and its two inverse homotopies with the transported class. The boundary-region stabilization is the literal old operator times the invertible constant factor, so it transports the same C-character. The relative compressionbody move word supplies the topology. On a zero-periodic homology-product branch C=0, and this paragraph specializes directly to the completed construction with no further choices. [construct]

4.1 **Keep a positive area form for the actual old pair.** Start with an actual weakly admissible (Σ,α,β). There is a positive area form ω annihilating every old periodic domain: separate the finite region coefficient subspace from the nonnegative orthant, then realize the resulting strictly positive region areas by positive smooth bumps and a sufficiently small positive background form. Fix this ω. Since ∂Σ≠∅, write ω=dλ. For a periodic domain Q, Stokes gives [construct]

4.2 area(Q)=∫∂Q λ. [construct]

4.3 This is an equality for signed two-chains, not a claim that every attaching circle is exact. Put A=span α, B=span β, C=A∩B as in the preceding construction. For u∈C the equality of α and β λ-periods follows exactly from old periodic area zero. [construct]

4.4 It suffices to construct γ and δ so that their λ-period functionals, expressed in the actual handle-slide bases of B, equal the β functional. Then every auxiliary periodic domain has area zero. Since the full triangle and quadrilateral domain groups are generated by the old C-domains and the auxiliary B-domains, every periodic domain of every required multidiagram has area zero. Positive ω then excludes a nonzero nonnegative periodic domain. This proves simultaneous weak admissibility, including auxiliary stabilizers, rather than inferring it from pairwise admissibility. [construct]

4.5 **An actual balanced slide patch.** Choose the slide band thin, with its interior disjoint from the other β circles. Its ribbon neighborhood is the actual planar two-handle patch used in the auxiliary unit construction. The four adjustable positive lobes have periodic domains [construct]

4.6 P₁=D₁−D₂−D₃,     P₂=D₃−D₄; [construct]

4.7 each spectator has P_i=E_i⁺−E_i⁻. Their span is all of the auxiliary B-domain group, not just the span of the sliding circle. This last fact follows also from the exact relation-group calculation for two copies of the same B: a domain is uniquely determined by its coefficient on one disk basis. [construct]

4.8 Construct the patch in area coordinates for the fixed ω. First make the band and all lobes so small that they lie in the chosen ribbon neighborhood. Prescribe [construct]

4.9 area(D₃)=area(D₄)=ε, area(D₂)=ε, area(D₁)=2ε, area(E_i⁺)=area(E_i⁻)>0. [construct]

4.10 These conditions are geometric choices, not a change of ω. To achieve them, reserve one subarc on each lobe boundary away from the intersections and the band junction. A normal displacement on that subarc changes its enclosed area continuously with nonzero derivative. The reserved subarcs have disjoint supports. Choose ε and the band width small first, then tune the remaining lobe areas in these subarcs. The D₃ band contribution is positive and can be made arbitrarily small; tune it first and then tune D₄, D₂, D₁ in that order. None of these displacements changes the crossing pattern, the slide-band isotopy class, or the strict convex corners. Spectator lobes are balanced by the same one-variable adjustment. The outside component continues to meet the actual boundary of Σ. [construct]

4.11 Thus ∫P₁ω=∫P₂ω=∫P_iω=0. Equivalently, the γ λ-periods are exactly the β λ-periods in the slid basis. The old C-periods have not changed: neither ω nor the old α,β circles was altered. Even if the ribbon patch crosses α circles, this statement remains true; its construction concerns the β-family only and the old periodic domains are still the original two-chains. [construct]

4.12 Choose δ as the small normal graph with the three-port placement used for the actual auxiliary triangle unit. Balance each positive and negative normal-graph lobe in ω-area. Then the βδ B-domains also have zero area. By subtraction so do the γδ domains. The three-port inequalities and the strict unit triangles remain valid: the area corrections occur along reserved open sides, away from the three ports and corners, and can be made arbitrarily small. Hence the same actual unit calculation is available on these simultaneously admissible diagrams. [construct]

4.13 For an elementary isotopy, use the same construction with a normal graph over the original circle: one positive lobe, one negative lobe of equal ω-area. It is an actual Hamiltonian deformation. Indeed, the normal velocity v_t along the moving circle satisfies ∫ι_{v_t}ω=0, because its λ-period is constant. Hence ι_{v_t}ω is the differential of a single-valued function on that circle. Extend that function to a thin annulus and cut it off outside; its Hamiltonian field has precisely the prescribed normal component. Different circles use disjoint annuli. [construct]

4.14 **Reaching prescribed diagrams rather than only specially balanced representatives.** A prescribed disk slide is represented by a slide band and a sufficiently small push-off; the balanced representative above uses that same band. Any other representative with the same band is isotopic to it. Thus it remains to realize a prescribed isotopy, not to assume that every representative is already action balanced. [construct]

4.15 Put the finite isotopy of one attaching family in generic position relative to the other. Its exceptional times are isolated ordinary tangencies creating or deleting a pair of intersections; between them the colored transverse curve graph has constant combinatorics. A compact isotopy can be approximated with finitely many such events. On an interval without an event, extend the velocity of the colored graph to an ambient vector field: at a crossing use the two transverse tangents as a basis, assigning their prescribed crossing-point velocity, then extend on the edges and patch in the complementary regions. Its flow carries the diagram exactly and carries the other family setwise. The induced surface diffeomorphism gives literal conjugacy of symmetric-product maps, operators, orientations, and domains after transporting J and ω. This step has no Hamiltonian or flux assumption. [construct]

4.16 At an exceptional event use its small disk normal form. Realize the creation/deletion by a sufficiently small normal bump of the moving circle. Add an opposite signed-area compensating bump on a different open subarc disjoint from the stationary family and every marked point. Such an arc exists because the intersection set is finite. Make the event disk small enough that its area is less than the capacity of the compensating strip. Vary that strip continuously so the total λ-period remains constant at every time. The compensating bump creates no intersection with the stationary family. Join the positive and negative graph portions with exactly two simple zeros. The resulting elementary move is Hamiltonian by the preceding primitive construction, and has exactly the required tangency event. Its endpoint and the prescribed local endpoint have the same colored graph, so the ambient-conjugacy step joins them. [construct]

4.17 This decomposes any prescribed finite isotopy into literal conjugacies and the admitted balanced elementary isotopies. Apply it also to the isotopy from a prescribed slide representative to the balanced representative of its band. No assertion that arbitrary non-Hamiltonian Lagrangian isotopies preserve Floer homology has been used. [construct]

4.18 **Actual consequence for the whole move word.** For each balanced elementary move, the complete finite triangle/quad configurations are weakly admissible by the fixed-positive-area argument. The signed exterior construction supplies their compactification. The transported C-character and the explicit K₄ extension supply their compatible signs. The actual auxiliary triangle is a unit, so the signed inverse and quadrilateral homotopies already constructed apply. Literal conjugacies transport the specified character. Ordinary stabilization is first converted by the relative geometry to the true boundary region and is then the literal old complex times its single invertible constant factor. [construct]

4.19 Consequently the relative compressionbody move word yields integral chain homotopy equivalences for the specified transported orientation class on general balanced sutured diagrams. The argument does not say that other C-characters produce the same homology. On the product/homology-product branch C=0, the character ambiguity disappears as previously proved. This supplies the new exterior move-admission operation required to use the nice cut diagram as an actual integral invariant, rather than only as a favorable chosen diagram. [construct] ∎
