## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an actual weakly admissible balanced sutured diagram on a surface with boundary, the integral disk complex exists for each specified coherent orientation class. Its disk, triangle and quadrilateral moduli spaces admit finite signed counts and the corresponding oriented boundary identities on actual weakly admissible multidiagrams. Sphere and one-torus boundary bubbles are excluded by the zero boundary-region multiplicities. Orientation classes are transported rather than declared equivalent.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-sutured-floer-chain-complex]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F2] [[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F3] [[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing]] is retained only at its complete multipointed S3-knot scope; it supplies no general incomplete sutured analytic framework. The actual sutured invocation is F5 below.

[F4] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F5] **External integral sutured analytic framework, in the classical full-Choice setting of F4.** For admissible balanced sutured diagrams, the actual incomplete attaching systems on a compact surface with boundary have the integral holomorphic-disk construction of Juhász, *Holomorphic discs and sutured manifolds*, AGT 6 (2006): §3, especially Definition 3.5 (zero multiplicity at every boundary region); Theorem 6.3, Corollary 6.4 and Lemma 6.5, printed pp.1444–1445 (domain-energy bound, compact rigid counts, and sphere/one-torus degeneration exclusion); Definition 7.1 and Theorems 7.2 and 7.5, pp.1445–1446 (coherently oriented integer differential, squared differential and admissible move invariance). The analytic framework referenced there is Ozsváth–Szabó, *Holomorphic disks and topological invariants for closed three-manifolds*, §§3.2–3.6 and §8.4: Fredholm sections for totally real product tori, regular perturbations, oriented compactifications and strip/triangle/quadrilateral gluing with its actual admissibility conditions. The sutured application uses zero multiplicity in every cap/boundary region and the actual periodic-domain/area and boundary-barrier checks made below; it is not a use of an S3-knot analytic theorem for incomplete attaching systems. For good admissible surface cuts, Juhász, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, GT12 (2008), Proposition7.6, printed pp.330–331, identifies the entire outer disk differential via actual conformal lifts of the rigid bigons/rectangles; the retained local determinant-splicing construction below fixes the specified integral orientation transport. These published analytic constructions are explicit external inputs under CLAUDF52, rather than a locally reconstructed general analytic theorem. Their source Statements do not assert a ZF+Countable-Choice foundation; no such axiom weakening is inferred here. [Juhász2006](https://msp.org/agt/2006/6-3/agt-v6-n3-p16-s.pdf), [Juhász2008](https://msp.org/gt/2008/12-1/gt-v12-n1-p07-s.pdf), [Ozsváth–Szabó](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0101206)

## Proof

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and the actual diagrams, markings, orientation classes, and admissibility hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 New operation, 2026-10-20. The argument below is a domain calculation. It is independent of determinant orientation choices and uses no manifold restriction. [construct]

1.2 Let $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\alpha,\beta)$ be a balanced sutured diagram. Let $Q$ be the region chain of a disk bubble whose whole boundary lies on $\mathbb T_\alpha$, rather than on alternating alpha and beta tori. Its boundary on the Heegaard surface is a sum of full alpha circles. There is no beta boundary: each beta segment therefore has equal coefficients on its two sides. Consequently the coefficient function of $Q$ is constant on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\bigcup\alpha$. Every such component meets $\partial\Sigma$ by balance, and a sutured domain has zero coefficient there. Thus every coefficient of $Q$ vanishes. The identical argument with alpha and beta exchanged handles beta bubbles. Nonnegativity and admissibility are not required for this calculation. [construct]

1.3 This also describes exactly why a closed-diagram one-torus disk cannot simply be carried into the sutured count: a positive component meeting a cap or deleted boundary region is not a sutured disk domain. The argument must be applied after imposing zero multiplicity at **every** sutured boundary component, not just at one selected closed-diagram basepoint. [construct]

1.4 On any actual sutured analytic construction for which the area identity for the operator and symplectic background in use gives energy zero to the zero domain, the above calculation excludes nonconstant alpha and beta bubbles. Compatibility with the almost complex structure then makes zero energy equivalent to constancy, since the energy density is nonnegative and strictly positive wherever the derivative is nonzero. Therefore those bubbles contribute no signed boundary strata at all. No comparison of alpha-bubble and beta-bubble signs is necessary in that setting. [construct]

1.5 The scope of this last implication is deliberate. The domain calculation does not itself construct an area identity for a new symmetric-product background, control sphere classes invisible to the domain map, or prove compactness of sutured moduli spaces. An accepted zero-domain area theorem can be invoked only when its actual target, area-form, divisor and boundary hypotheses hold. It must not be extended from complete closed Heegaard data to arbitrary incomplete sutured systems merely because the same curves can be drawn on a capped surface. Signed strip breaking, triangle/rectangle compatibility, and signed move maps remain separate constructions. [construct]

2.1 New signed construction, 2026-10-20. This concerns an actual chosen diagram whose periodic-domain lattice is zero. It applies to the actual product-cut diagram, and to the rank-one homology-product branch after the earlier determinant reduction. It is not a claim of signed invariance on every general sutured diagram. [construct]

2.2 **Analytic input and the new sign operation.** Supply the actual strip Fredholm realizations with transverse ends, orientability on each map-space component from the framed attaching-torus construction, and the actual linear sewing estimates for sufficiently long matching ends. These are operator/gluing inputs, not integer count identities. In particular a finite cokernel can be killed by finitely many compactly supported target sections; the resulting onto operators have bounded right inverses, and sewing their kernels by cutoff and projection is an isomorphism for long necks. No orientation of that isomorphism is presumed. The following defines it explicitly and checks the needed coherence. [construct]

2.3 For $D_i$ choose an ordered finite-dimensional space $V_i$ of added domain columns making $\widetilde D_i$ onto, and write $K_i=\ker\widetilde D_i$. Use the determinant model [construct]

2.4 $$\det D_i=\det K_i\otimes(\det V_i)^*.$$ [construct]

2.5 For a sewn operator append $V_1\oplus V_2$ in that order. Let $Q_T$ be a right inverse of the augmented sewn operator, and let $\operatorname{pre}_T$ be cutoff sewing on sections and the identity on the finite variables. Its actual kernel comparison is [construct]

2.6 $$G_T(k_1,k_2)=(1-Q_T\widetilde D_T)\operatorname{pre}_T(k_1,k_2).$$ [construct]

2.7 The supplied sewing estimate makes this an isomorphism $K_1\oplus K_2\to\ker\widetilde D_T$ for large $T$. Transport the wedge orientation through this map, with all $K$ factors in component order and then all dual $V$ factors in component order. When moving $V_1^*$ past $K_2$, insert the actual exterior-algebra sign $(-1)^{\dim V_1\dim K_2}$. This defines the determinant-splicing map, including its sign. It is not obtained from an unsigned count. [construct]

2.8 The construction is independent of finite stabilization. Adding an extra column space $W$ changes the kernel determinant by the exact-sequence factor $\det W$ and adds its dual $\det W^*$; contract these adjacent factors using the ordered evaluation pairing. A finite block decomposition into the old kernel, its invertible complement, and the new columns proves this identity even when some new columns land in the old range. Passing to a common stabilization therefore compares any two choices. Varying right inverses causes no sign ambiguity: their space is affine, and the cutoff/projection maps remain isomorphisms for long enough necks uniformly on each compact interpolation path. A continuous nonzero real determinant has constant sign. [construct]

2.9 For three components, use disjoint matching necks and append $V_1,V_2,V_3$ once in that order. Both parenthesizations tend, in the common kernel coordinates, to the same cutoff-sewn direct sum $K_1\oplus K_2\oplus K_3$. Their relative finite-dimensional operator tends to the identity; hence for both necks sufficiently long it lies in the identity component of the invertible matrices. Both exterior-algebra reorderings also give the same final factor order, so their Koszul signs agree. This proves associativity of the actual determinant-splicing maps. The same argument works for any finite number of necks. Shortening a neck within a fixed component transports this identification by determinant-line continuation; it is not a new arbitrary sign choice. [construct]

2.10 For sphere insertion one can construct the needed determinant identification by compact operator excision, without assuming a regular holomorphic sphere gluing theorem. Choose an interior disk on each component, identify their collar bundles by complex frames, and deform their zeroth-order coefficients there to the same standard complex-linear coefficients. This is an affine deformation of actual Cauchy--Riemann operators with unchanged principal symbol and strip ends; determinant orientations transport along it. Cut across the common collars in the two pairs $P\oplus A_S$ and $P\#S\oplus A_0$, where $A_S$ is the closed-sphere operator and $A_0$ the trivial-bundle sphere operator. Rotate the two matching exterior traces by the real two-by-two rotation $R_\theta$, from identity to the exchange at $\theta=\pi/2$. Real multiplication by $R_\theta$ commutes with the common complex symbol. A collar cutoff identifies all transmission domains; after this identification the operator changes only by compactly supported zeroth-order terms. Thus this is an actual continuous Fredholm family, furnishing the orientation excision identification between the two displayed direct sums. Stabilizing by finite target sections gives its determinant model exactly as above. The sphere factors have canonical complex orientations: homotope their real-linear zeroth-order terms to a complex-linear Cauchy--Riemann operator in the contractible affine space of such terms. Its kernel and cokernel are complex vector spaces, and complex orientations cannot change along a complex-linear family. The factor $A_0$ is the complex matching-fiber factor, of real index $2m$. [construct]

2.11 For several sphere cuts choose disjoint collars. Their trace rotations commute, giving the same determinant orientation on either route around the parameter square. Exchanging sphere factors likewise has positive Koszul sign because their real indices and the real index $2m$ of each matching factor are even. Consequently insertion of spheres commutes with strip splicing, and successive insertions use the canonical complex orientation of their sum. This is an operator-orientation construction, not an assertion that a holomorphic sphere bubble or regular nonlinear sphere-gluing chart exists. [construct]

2.12 **Assign the orientations without assuming a general-Y normalization.** Assume now the periodic-domain lattice is zero. In each connected component of the finite-generator Whitney groupoid choose a base generator $x_0$ and a reference class $\theta_x:x_0\to x$ for every object, with $\theta_{x_0}$ constant. Choose an orientation of each reference determinant component. These are finitely many choices. Their extensions over each component are well-defined by the supplied framed-torus orientability construction. [construct]

2.13 For any class $u:x\to y$, the composite $\theta_x*u*\theta_y^{-1}$ has zero domain because it is periodic and the periodic-domain group vanishes. By the explicit capping argument in the orientation-character donor, this composite is a sphere insertion. Its sphere class is unique: the two boundary caps lie in product tori, and $\pi_2$ of those tori is zero, so changing the caps cannot add a sphere class. Equivalently, the sphere-to-Whitney-class map is injective by this same cap construction. Therefore write [construct]

2.14 $$u=\theta_x^{-1}*S(u)*\theta_y.$$ [construct]

2.15 Orient its determinant using the chosen reference orientations, the inverse reference orientation determined by the constant class, and the canonical complex orientation of $S(u)$. The splicing map constructed above makes this an orientation of the actual determinant component. There is no hidden orientation assigned by a formal sign of a domain: the domain is used only to identify the remaining class as a sphere, and the determinant orientation is transported through actual operator splicing. [construct]

2.16 For composable classes $u:x\to y$, $v:y\to z$, the two adjacent reference factors $\theta_y$ and $\theta_y^{-1}$ contract to the positive constant factor. Associativity and the even complex sphere factors then give $o(u*v)=o(u)\wedge o(v)$ under the actual splicing map. Sphere insertions retain their canonical orientation. This is a coherent strip orientation system on the zero-periodic diagram. A change of reference choices gives only generator sign changes, by the earlier exact character classification. Neither $S^3$ nor an absolute Maslov normalization appears. [construct]

2.17 **What follows for a supplied compactified strip problem.** Suppose the actual zero/one-dimensional strip moduli for this diagram are regular and compactified, and the only boundary strata of the index-two translation quotients are broken pairs of index-one strips. The new coherent orientations orient those compact one-manifolds. In a gluing chart choose the global translation coordinate $s$ and neck separation $T$ so the two component translations are $s_1=s-T/2$, $s_2=s+T/2$. The Jacobian is $+1$, so $ds_1\wedge ds_2=ds\wedge dT$. After quotienting by the positively oriented translation, the endpoint sign of a broken pair is one fixed convention factor times the product of its two rigid-strip signs. That convention factor is the same at every broken pair in the coefficient under consideration. The signed boundary count of a compact oriented one-manifold is zero. Consequently every integer coefficient of $\partial^2$ is zero. [construct]

2.18 One-torus degenerations have zero domain by the separate balanced-domain calculation. They are absent wherever the actual zero-domain energy identity applies. Sphere bubbles must likewise be excluded using the actual analytic hypotheses, rather than by falsely asserting $\pi_2(\operatorname{Sym}^d\Sigma)=0$. The construction above is compatible with canonical sphere orientations but does not replace that exclusion. Thus this paragraph supplies the signed boundary identity once the stated compactification hypotheses have actually been met. [construct]

2.19 **Extend over a triangle with two zero-periodic boundary pairs.** There is a further specific extension relevant to a move between two product-cut diagrams. Suppose a triple $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ has zero periodic-domain groups for the main pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ and $(\alpha,\gamma)$. Supply a coherent system on its auxiliary pair $(\beta,\gamma)$, as well as the systems just constructed on the main pairs. Supply orientability of the triangle determinant components and the actual linear sewing problems at their three strip ends. Their determinant identifications are given the finite-stabilization sign convention above. [construct]

2.20 Fix any orbit of triangle classes under splicing boundary disks. Its stabilizers have no nontrivial domain relation: if periodic boundary disks $u_{\alpha\beta},u_{\beta\gamma},u_{\alpha\gamma}$ return a triangle to the same class, then their signed domain sum is zero. The first and third domains are zero by hypothesis, so the auxiliary domain is zero as well. The capping argument makes all three disks sphere insertions. The residual sphere sum acts trivially only when it is the zero sphere class: cap the three boundary loops in their aspherical product tori, whose second homotopy groups vanish. Its determinant action therefore has positive complex orientation, by the sphere excision construction. Thus no stabilizer can reverse a triangle orientation. [construct]

2.21 Choose an orientation of one determinant component per orbit and extend it by the three boundary-disk systems, using the actual splicing maps. The stabilizer calculation proves that this extension is independent of the representative. Associativity of the finite kernel sewing maps proves compatibility with all further disk insertions. The choices require at most Countable Choice: homotopy classes of maps between the finite CW models in use are countable, and the set of generator triples is finite. This constructs compatible triangle orientation systems under the stated actual operator-orientability/sewing inputs. It does not claim the auxiliary orientation system exists merely because the two main pairs have no periodic domains. [construct]

2.22 In particular this shows why the general-Y strip orientation-character issue does **not** by itself obstruct a triangle joining two homology-product cut diagrams. It also locates the next problem more narrowly. For the inverse-homotopy quadrilateral one must align the three auxiliary pair systems and auxiliary triangle system, not simply orient another isolated triangle component. A relation among those auxiliary periodic classes can remain even though every main pair has zero periodic domains. Such a relation is absent from the two-main-pair stabilizer calculation just proved; it cannot be removed by repeating that calculation for the two triangulations separately. [construct]

3.1 New construction, 2026-10-20. Start with an actual admissible balanced sutured diagram. The surface may have arbitrary genus and several boundary components, and its attaching systems need not be complete systems on a closed surface. The target below is closed only to obtain a compact analytic ambient space. No closed-manifold invariance assertion is imported for the incomplete attaching systems. [construct]

3.2 **1. Construct the actual compact target and its area identity.** Cap every boundary circle of $\Sigma$ by a disk, obtaining a closed Riemann surface $\bar\Sigma$. Retain a point $z_j$ in each cap and a small open collar of the old boundary in the cap-plus-surface. All attaching circles miss these collars. Put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^d\bar\Sigma$, with the actual $d$ of the sutured diagram, not the genus of $\bar\Sigma$. Its product tori are compact, embedded and disjoint from the discriminant. They have their ordered global tangent frames. [construct]

3.3 Choose positive region areas annihilating the sutured periodic-domain subspace. The finite positive-area separation argument applies exactly because admissibility excludes nonzero nonnegative periodic chains; it imposes no rational-homology-sphere assumption. Realize the areas by a smooth positive surface form: start with a sufficiently small positive background form and add a nonnegative smooth bump inside each of the finitely many regions to reach its prescribed integral. Extend it positively over the caps. Call the result $\omega_\Sigma$. [construct]

3.4 The product form on $\bar\Sigma^d$ descends to a smooth Kähler form away from the discriminant and to a continuous-potential positive current $T$ everywhere. To construct a smooth form while preserving the tori, use the following local smoothing. In a cluster coordinate disk take a smooth strictly subharmonic potential $f$ for $\omega_\Sigma$. The symmetric potential is $F(s)=\sum_i f(z_i)$ in the elementary symmetric coordinates $s$ of its roots. It is continuous and plurisubharmonic; on a compact cluster chart it is strictly so. Indeed the quotient polynomial map has bounded derivative there, so $\sum f(z_i)-\varepsilon|s(z)|^2$ remains plurisubharmonic for sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$. Positivity descends through the finite quotient, including its branch locus by continuity. Local differences of these potentials are smooth pluriharmonic functions: they are sums of real parts of holomorphic functions of the roots, hence symmetric holomorphic functions of $s$. [construct]

3.5 Mollify these strictly plurisubharmonic potentials on smaller charts. Paste replacements using a smooth regularized maximum, chosen to equal the larger entry when their difference exceeds its smoothing width. Strict positivity has a positive margin on each compact chart, so choose the mollification error and maximum width below that margin. Give each replacement a small positive offset on its inner chart and a negative offset on its outer collar; the maximum then selects the smooth replacement inside and the old potential near the collar. A finite nested chart cover of the compact discriminant makes these replacements smooth everywhere. Outside that cover leave the old potential unchanged. The resulting smooth Kähler form $\omega$ equals the product form on neighborhoods of **all** attaching tori; its difference from $T$ is $dd^c\psi$ for a global continuous potential supported in that cover. Thus the attaching tori remain Lagrangian. This construction keeps the actual target dimension $d$ throughout. [construct]

3.6 For a strip or polygon standard-holomorphic near the discriminant and with boundary on those tori, the area is [construct]

3.7 $$\int u^*\omega=\sum_R n_R(u)\int_R\omega_\Sigma.$$ [construct]

3.8 Here is the relative, rather than purely absolute, reason. The incidence cover records the individual roots of the configuration; its evaluation to the surface pushes its oriented fundamental chain to the region domain, so integration against $\omega_\Sigma$ is the right-hand side. Off the branch locus this is literally the product-form integral. Near the branch locus the map is standard holomorphic, and the continuous symmetric potential pulls back with positive Hölder exponent; excising small disks there produces boundary integrals tending to zero. Stokes therefore computes the correction by $\psi$ only on the strip/polygon boundary and its ends. That correction is zero because $\psi$ vanishes on neighborhoods of all tori. The same argument on a sphere gives $\int v^*\omega=\operatorname{area}(\bar\Sigma)\,n_z(v)$ for any point divisor. It does not assert that all zero-domain sphere homotopy classes are trivial. [construct]

3.9 **2. Impose every cap condition and exclude the extra degenerations.** Use almost complex data equal to the symmetric integrable structure near the discriminant, near the finitely many point divisors of one test point in **each** complementary region, and near every point-divisor $E_p$ with $p$ in the cap-plus-boundary collars. Count only classes with $n_{z_j}=0$ for **every** cap. These conditions are additive under breaking. A divisor crossing in those standard neighborhoods has positive local multiplicity. The degree is constant as $p$ moves within a complementary boundary region, so zero cap multiplicity forces zero multiplicity for every collar test point. If a coordinate entered a collar, the standard-holomorphic incidence evaluation there would have positive local degree at some test point. Thus every counted map stays in the fixed compact subtarget with no coordinate in those collars. This gives the actual sutured boundary barrier, rather than merely placing one marked point on a capped drawing. [construct]

3.10 The domain coefficients are nonnegative by point-divisor positivity, with zero coefficient on all boundary regions. For fixed endpoints their differences are sutured periodic domains. The finite integer-domain bound follows from admissibility: an unbounded sequence of nonnegative domains, normalized by its norm, would converge to a nonzero nonnegative vector in the real periodic subspace; rational approximation in that rational subspace would give a forbidden integral periodic domain. Hence the domains and, by the displayed area identity, their energies are bounded. [construct]

3.11 Every nonconstant sphere bubble is excluded in the compactification. Its cap degrees are nonnegative and sum to zero, so they vanish. Point-divisor classes are homologous on the closed surface, so its degree at every point divisor is zero; the actual sphere area identity makes its energy zero. A tame holomorphic map with zero energy is constant. A one-torus boundary bubble has zero sutured domain by the balanced complementary-component argument already supplied. The relative area identity likewise makes it constant. These arguments treat the actual smoothing and its actual target, so they do not extend a zero-area statement to an unrelated background. [construct]

3.12 **3. Supply coherent orientations with nonzero periodic domains.** The previous determinant-splicing construction gives actual associative signed line maps using finite cokernel columns, cutoff/projection kernel maps and the exterior-algebra factor order. Individual disk components are orientable because the two product-torus tangent bundles have global ordered frames. To extend from the zero-periodic branch to the actual exterior, one additional commutator calculation is required. [construct]

3.13 Let $\Lambda$ be the actual image of the periodic Whitney group in the finite integral periodic-domain lattice. It is a finitely generated free abelian group. Choose a basis and represented periodic classes $p_i$ lifting it. All periodic classes have even index, by the actual endpoint intersection-sign parity identity at the same generator. The kernel of the domain map is exactly sphere insertion, with its canonical complex orientation. [construct]

3.14 The orientation commutator of two lifted periodic classes is positive. An explicit comparison uses their boundary loops in each product torus. Homotope those loops to their linear winding representatives in $\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$. Their commutator contracts through the square $(s,t)\mapsto x+s a+t b$ in that torus. The global tangent frame extends across this **actual** square. Cut the four disk operators and these two torus squares into common collar pieces. The constant real-boundary square operator has its canonical ordered $\mathbb R^d$ determinant factor; the matching real-fiber factors cancel with their ordered duals. The two ways to reassemble differ by exchanging the two disk determinant factors and by the capped sphere operator. The exchange sign is $(-1)^{\operatorname{ind}p_i\operatorname{ind}p_j}=+1$, and the sphere factor has its positive complex orientation. There is no additional framing loop: both torus squares were filled in their global frames. This computes the commutator sign, rather than assuming a free abelian domain lattice automatically splits an arbitrary sign extension. [construct]

3.15 Choose orientations for the finitely many $p_i$ and the finitely many reference generator paths in each Whitney-groupoid component. For a general class, subtract its reference paths and ordered powers of the $p_i$; the remainder is a unique sphere insertion. Orient using those factors and the canonical sphere factor. Any reordering uses exactly the positive commutator just computed, inverses contract to the constant orientation, and the determinant associator is already fixed. Therefore the construction is independent of the word and compatible with every disk splice. It supplies an actual coherent strip orientation system for this chosen admissible exterior diagram. Changing the periodic choices has exactly the character ambiguity previously derived; this construction does not assert all such choices yield the same group. [construct]

3.16 **4. Realize the signed finite complexes and parameter boundaries.** At this point the actual problem has compact target containment, totally real compact attaching tori, transverse generator ends, bounded energies, the boundary/cap barrier, and the preceding sphere/one-torus degeneration exclusions. Invoke the exact sutured operator framework [F5] for these admitted strip and polygon problems, retaining the integrable collars, the zero boundary-region multiplicities and the verified periodic-domain conditions. This is the needed external pointwise Fredholm/regularity, compactification and strip/triangle/quadrilateral gluing input for incomplete balanced sutured systems. The S3-knot supplier [F3] is not used to enlarge its scope. The explicit determinant and sign constructions in sections2–3 then orient these actual compactifications and their boundary/gluing maps as stated, without replacing them by unsigned counts. This invocation is in the full-Choice background F4; a Countable-Choice application needs a separately justified specialization of these pointwise analytic constructions and cannot follow merely by changing a metadata edge or counting diagram classes. [F5, F4, construct]

3.17 Choose generic actual strip data and polygon/parameter data inductively, preserving already chosen regular ends. On a finite collection of geometric moves there are only finitely many diagram families; the homotopy-class inventory is countable. The parametric regularity construction is applied relative to the prescribed ends and the frozen divisor/diagonal neighborhoods. Nonconstant maps have mobile points outside those frozen neighborhoods: otherwise unique continuation would make them constant on the open end neighborhoods and hence everywhere. The known framed product generator models handle constant ends. This is where the actual compact-target Sard--Smale and gluing input is needed; the finite area calculation alone is not a regularity theorem. [construct]

3.18 The zero-dimensional counts are finite. The index-two translation quotients and the corresponding one-dimensional triangle/quadrilateral parameter moduli compactify only by the indicated broken polygons, because the actual cap/area argument has removed the other bubbles. Coherent determinant orientations give their signed boundary identities. In particular $\partial^2=0$ over $\mathbb Z$, the actual triangle operators are chain maps, and the compatible quadrilateral has the identity $GF-U=dH+Hd$. Use the newly constructed auxiliary top unit and the finite signed small-isotopy inverse to obtain the explicit left/right inverse homotopies already supplied. No mod-two cancellation is used at this stage. [construct]

3.19 For the chosen local auxiliary ends, the regular integrable bigons, annular matching solutions and product triangles persist under sufficiently small generic perturbations: the implicit function theorem continues each regular isolated solution, and the new energy/bubble bounds prevent additional sequences from appearing without an integrable limit in the exhaustive local list. Hence the prescribed regular unit count can be retained while choosing the mixed exterior families. This is a choice of actual compatible data, not an assertion that arbitrary unaligned endpoint data have already been compared. [construct]

3.20 **5. Align actual strip choices, including their generator jets.** For two chosen tame strip data on the same capped target, first keep the same symplectic form and the same attaching tori. Join their almost complex data through tame data fixed on the divisor/discriminant neighborhoods. Such a path can be chosen pointwise in the Cayley ball based at a fixed compatible structure: the anti-complex-linear Cayley parameter has norm less than one, and radial contraction to zero followed by expansion gives the required path. The common protected values stay fixed. The data need not initially have identical generator jets. [construct]

3.21 Every constant continuation strip at a generator is regular. Its linearization is $\xi_s+J_{s,t}(x)\xi_t$, with the two fixed transverse linear Lagrangian planes and zero limits. The zeroth-order derivative-of-$J$ term is zero because the underlying map is constant. A kernel section has linear symplectic area zero: the standard linear Liouville form vanishes on either plane, and the end terms vanish. The equation gives $\xi_t=J_{s,t}(x)\xi_s$, so tameness makes this area the integral of a strictly positive quadratic form in $\xi_s$. Hence $\xi=0$. Its Fredholm index is zero by deformation to the constant-coefficient transverse operator, so its cokernel is zero as well. This is an actual kernel argument, not an assumption that arbitrary endpoint jet changes preserve regularity. [construct]

3.22 Use actual generic continuation data relative to these regular constant strips. The cap barrier, area bound and bubble exclusions apply unchanged. Orient their index-zero operators by determinant continuation from the chosen endpoint systems; the constant strip has coefficient $+1$ with the identity convention. Index-one continuation compactifications give the signed chain-map identity. For a reverse path, stretch and then contract the concatenation through a two-parameter continuation family. Its compact oriented one-dimensional boundary has the composite, the constant-path identity, and broken strips. The same determinant/corner orientation convention therefore gives actual chain homotopies $RC-1=dK+Kd$ and $CR-1=dK'+K'd$. Every map and parameter count in this argument is on the chosen sutured compact-target problem of sections 1--4, not a use of a closed-system invariance conclusion. [construct]

3.23 With an annihilating area form there is also a finite explicit inverse for the continuation matrix. In each Whitney-groupoid component assign a generator the area of a reference disk from a base generator. Periodic domains and zero-cap sphere insertions have zero area, so differences of those assigned values are unambiguous. A nonconstant continuation has strictly positive area and moves strictly in that finite action order. The constant solutions give the diagonal identity. Thus its matrix is $1+N$ with $N$ strictly triangular, and its integer inverse is the finite alternating sum $1-N+N^2-\cdots$. This supplements, rather than replaces, the parameter-family homotopy proof. [construct]

3.24 To align choices constructed using different positive surface forms, compare each endpoint at its **own** form to a sufficiently small perturbation of the symmetric integrable structure. For a finite list of forms, those reference perturbations can be chosen tame for all of their smoothed Kähler forms, since the common integrable structure has a positive tameness margin on their compact targets. At a shared diagram fix one such form and use the preceding continuation construction to compare the reference data there. This does not require an arbitrary original endpoint to be tame for a foreign form. If target complex charts are held fixed, the construction aligns the actual forms and generator jets needed at the junctions of a finite move word. [construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the analytic existence and invariant chain-comparison assertions. Let a balanced sutured manifold be taut. For a specified coherent orientation class, its integral sutured Floer homology has a direct summand isomorphic to the integers. More precisely, a finite good taut hierarchy terminating in product balls induces a split inclusion of the terminal product homology into the original homology, with orientation classes induced along the cuts.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. It is assumed when invoking existence, regularity, compactification, and invariant comparison maps from the imported integral sutured analytic framework. The finite domain and determinant calculations retain their stated conditional supplied-data hypotheses; no unconditional Countable-Choice analytic existence theorem is asserted. In particular the Countable-Choice selection result applies only GIVEN its actual pointwise operator constructions, not merely because the diagrams or domain classes are countable.

[F1] [[thm-balanced-taut-sutured-manifolds-admit-finite-good-hierarchies]] supplies the actual finite good taut hierarchy with its terminal product balls.

[F2] [[lem-signed-relative-surface-cut-and-horizontal-decomposition]] supplies the actual signed outer-to-cut chain isomorphism, retaining nonzero periodic domains by pullback of the specified orientation character.

[F3] [[lem-relative-sutured-diagrams-have-signed-move-equivalences]] compares actual sutured diagrams with the specified transported orientation class and computes a product by its empty diagram.

[F4] [[lem-signed-essential-product-annulus-decomposition]] gives literal product one-handle and disk complex identifications.

## Proof

**Given:** A taut balanced sutured manifold and a specified coherent orientation class on its finite admissible integral chain complex. The Axiom of Choice is assumed for the analytic invocations [A1]; the relative finite-move geometry and supplied finite-complex algebra keep their stated inputs.

1.1 For a good cut surface S and its actual adapted polygon P, choose the standard fixed boundary vector field and a frame of its orthogonal plane along the one-dimensional boundary of S. Such a frame always exists along those circles; no global trivialization of the plane over the entire boundary is assumed. Let c(S) be the relative Euler obstruction for the outer local Morse field. Replacing that field along an interior generator trajectory adds two positive turns on S, one on either side of its trajectory tube. Boundary creases contribute the fixed tangent Euler, half-suture-crossing and boundary rotation terms to c(S); they are independent of the generator. Therefore the relative plane Euler obstruction of a generator x on S is c(S)+2n_P(x), where n_P counts its interior polygon coordinates. In particular it has the outer value exactly when n_P(x)=0. [construct]

1.2 This relative obstruction depends only on the relative Spin^c class of x. Indeed, equality of those classes means the nonvanishing generator vector fields are homotopic outside an interior ball, with their fixed boundary values. Push S off that ball and restrict the homotopy of orthogonal planes to S. Its framed boundary is unchanged, so the relative Euler obstruction is unchanged. Equivalently, changing the field in its relative Spin^c class changes neither the paired obstruction nor the fixed crease contributions. Thus a relative Spin^c class contains either only outer generators or none. This is the required class-level assertion; it is stronger than merely calling the outer generator set a subset. [step 1.1, construct]

1.3 The differential preserves relative Spin^c classes. For a disk, its α and β trace boundary gives a nullhomologous generator-difference cycle; modifying the Morse field along that bounding trace supplies the relative homotopy outside a ball. Consequently the whole chain complex is the direct sum of its relative Spin^c subcomplexes, and the outer complex is the direct sum of a subset of them by step 1.2. The projection onto this subset is a chain retraction of its inclusion. In particular its homology is a direct summand of the whole homology over the integers, with no field or torsion-freeness assumption. [step 1.2, construct]

1.4 Take the actual finite hierarchy of F1. At each cut use its good adapted admissible nice representative and F2 with the orientation character induced from the previous stage. The resulting cut homology identifies with the outer summand at that stage. Combining its chain inclusion and retraction with the signed diagram equivalences of F3 gives a split inclusion on homology from the next stage to the preceding stage. Auxiliary product one-handles or product disks in the hierarchy use the literal identifications of F4. None of these maps replaces the specified orientation class by an arbitrary one. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.3]

1.5 The terminal disjoint product balls have empty diagrams. Their disjoint union has the single product empty tuple, zero differential and integral homology Z. Its determinant line has the empty-product orientation. Compose the finitely many homology inclusions from step 1.4 and compose the retractions in the reverse order. Their composite on the terminal Z is the identity. Thus Z is an actual direct summand of the original integral homology. [F3, step 1.4] ∎

## Statement

Let a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented three-manifold be fibered with a specified connected oriented Seifert fiber. Its compact exterior with two meridional sutures admits a good surface-adapted balanced diagram carrying that actual Seifert surface, its boundary longitude, and the meridional boundary trivialization. For a fiber of an actual open book the cut/double diagram represents the marked product obtained by cutting along the fiber, with the original monodromy retained in regluing.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-sutured-floer-chain-complex]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F2] [[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F3] [[def-knot-relative-spinc-structure]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

## Proof

**Given:** The actual diagrams, markings, orientation classes, and admissibility hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 New topological construction, 2026-10-20. This replaces the unverified two-marking of the unchanged doubled-page diagram. It constructs a diagram of the actual meridionally sutured exterior and retains the actual fiber. It makes no claim that the resulting attaching systems have the old upper-page intersection pattern. [construct]

1.2 **Input and output.** Let $F$ be a compact connected oriented genus-$g$ surface with one boundary component, and let $\phi:F\to F$ be an orientation-preserving return diffeomorphism equal to the identity in a specified boundary collar. Use the actual open-book manifold: start with the mapping torus of $\phi$ and attach $\partial F\times D^2$ so the angular coordinate of $D^2$ is the mapping-torus coordinate. Its binding is $K=\partial F\times\{0\}$. The completed pages at angles $0$ and $\pi$ form the doubled-page splitting surface $\Sigma_0$ of genus $2g$. Denote its two actual handlebodies by $H_\alpha,H_\beta$. Their complete disk systems are the doubled cocores of a disk-band presentation of $F$. All these statements refer to the supplied open-book model, not merely to an arbitrary diagram with the right number of curves. [construct]

1.3 The construction produces a surface $\Sigma=\Sigma_0\setminus(\operatorname{int}D_p\cup\operatorname{int}D_q)$, with two boundary components, and $2g$ complete attaching circles in each family. Its balanced sutured manifold is exactly $Y\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ with two oppositely oriented meridional sutures. The original fiber, carried through the specified isotopy, is retained as a properly embedded surface whose boundary meets these sutures once each. Cutting along that surface is the marked product $F\times[0,1]$ with the return map retained on its ends. [construct]

1.4 **1. Bridge the actual seam.** Choose distinct points $p,q$ on the binding seam in $\Sigma_0$. They divide the seam into two closed arcs $a_\alpha,a_\beta$ with common endpoints and disjoint interiors. In a two-sided product collar of $\Sigma_0$, push the interior of $a_\alpha$ a small distance into $H_\alpha$ and the interior of $a_\beta$ into $H_\beta$. Use a positive smooth displacement vanishing at the endpoints; round in disjoint coordinate balls at $p,q$. The result is an embedded knot $K'$ ambient isotopic to $K$: in the collar, interpolate the displacement linearly from zero, and extend that explicit small graph isotopy using the collar's normal coordinate and a compact cutoff. Carry the pages and their normal framing by this same isotopy. [construct]

1.5 Each pushed arc $k_\alpha\subset H_\alpha$ and $k_\beta\subset H_\beta$ has an actual bridge disk: sweep its original boundary arc through this collar displacement. The swept rectangle, with its two endpoint sides collapsed and rounded, is an embedded disk whose boundary consists of the pushed arc and the original arc on $\Sigma_0$. Thus the arcs are boundary parallel in the specified handlebodies. This is an isotopy of the actual binding, not an identification inferred from basepoint positions. [construct]

1.6 **2. Construct disk systems missing the bridge arcs.** Here is the finite disk-patch operation needed on either handlebody $H$. Let $a\subset\partial H$ be its boundary bridge arc. Choose a smooth disk patch $D\subset\partial H$ containing $a$ in its interior, and choose a slightly larger disk patch $D^+$. Start with the supplied complete compressing disks. Select a point in $\operatorname{int}D$ outside their finitely many boundary circles and a small disk $D_0$ about that point disjoint from those circles. [construct]

1.7 There is an explicit boundary isotopy shrinking $D$ into $D_0$. Choose a disk coordinate on $D^+$, first carry its chosen center to the origin through a small coordinate flow, and then use radial maps $r\mapsto f_t(r)$ with $f_t'>0$, fixed near $\partial D^+$, shrinking the smaller disk into $D_0$. The increasing functions can be chosen by integrating a positive smooth radial derivative and normalizing its total integral; leave it equal to one near the outside boundary. This gives a surface diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity. Extend its time-dependent vector field to a collar of $\partial H$, multiply by a cutoff in the normal coordinate, and integrate it on the compact handlebody. This gives an actual handlebody isotopy with that boundary value. [construct]

1.8 Pull the old complete disk system back by its endpoint diffeomorphism. Its boundary circles now miss $D$, and its complement remains the original cut ball carried by a diffeomorphism. Choose a sufficiently thin boundary collar and straighten the disks there as products of their boundary curves. Their interiors away from that collar are compact, so the bridge disk and arc can be chosen in the collar over $D$, disjoint from every compressing disk. Equivalently, first make this collar choice and then perform the arbitrarily small bridge push of section 1. No endpoint of the final binding is moved by an unrecorded identification: the auxiliary boundary isotopy only constructs the new disks, while the bridge arcs remain the specified arcs of $K'$. [construct]

1.9 Perform this operation independently in $H_\alpha$ and $H_\beta$. Let the new disk boundaries be $\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta$. Both systems miss small common disks $D_p,D_q$ around the endpoints, because their boundary curves miss their respective bridge patches containing both endpoints. Make the two attaching systems transverse by small boundary perturbations away from these endpoint disks; carry their disk witnesses at the same time. This preparation need not preserve any old intersections. [construct]

1.10 **3. Drill and read the actual sutures.** Delete a small product neighborhood of each pushed bridge arc from its handlebody. The two deleted neighborhoods fit at the endpoint disks to the actual tubular neighborhood $N(K')$ with the carried page framing. Each new complete disk system misses its arc neighborhood. Cutting its drilled handlebody along those disks gives a ball with a boundary-parallel arc neighborhood removed, hence a solid torus. This last identification is explicit in a bridge-disk neighborhood: a ball with the neighborhood of a diameter-parallel proper arc removed is an annulus times an interval, after rounding. The meridian disks that were cut remain the feet of the original $2g$ one-handles. [construct]

1.11 Consequently each drilled handlebody is the compression body obtained from an annulus times an interval by attaching $2g$ one-handles. Its positive boundary is precisely $\Sigma$; its negative annulus $A_\alpha$ or $A_\beta$ is the tube around its bridge arc. Compressing $\Sigma$ along the corresponding attaching circles gives that annulus. In particular every component of the complement of a single attaching system meets $\partial\Sigma$, so the diagram is balanced. This can also be read from the original cut sphere with the two endpoint disks deleted: it is an annulus, and cutting the attaching curves only adds the retained disk faces. [construct]

1.12 Glue the two drilled compression bodies along their original punctured splitting surface. Since the bridge isotopy and tube matching were explicit, the result is literally the exterior of $K'$, hence is ambient diffeomorphic to the exterior of the original binding. Its torus boundary is $A_\alpha\cup A_\beta$, joined along the two endpoint meridian circles. Choose the two sutured annuli as narrow collars of these joining circles. The remaining two annuli are $R_-$ and $R_+$. Each joining circle bounds a normal disk in the deleted tube at $p$ or $q$, so it is an actual meridian of $K'$. Their induced suture orientations are opposite. This proves the required peripheral marking; a longitude has not been substituted for a meridian. [construct]

1.13 **4. Retain the actual fiber class.** Carry a completed open-book page through the bridge isotopy and delete its boundary collar inside $N(K')$. The resulting surface $F'$ is properly embedded in the constructed exterior. In the carried page framing of $N(K')$, its boundary is the longitude with fixed normal angle. Each endpoint meridian circle meets it once, with the two sutured crossings having opposite boundary-region directions. Thus $F'$ is the actual decomposing Seifert surface, not an inferred polygon on $\Sigma$. [construct]

1.14 The complement of a binding tube in the original open book is the supplied mapping torus of the truncated page. Carry this model by the same ambient isotopy. Cutting at $F'$ opens the base circle to an interval and yields the marked product $F\times[0,1]$. At its two ends the original return map is still $\phi$; no assertion that $\phi$ is isotopic to the identity is used. The construction covers $g=0$ as well: the doubled splitting is a sphere, there are no attaching circles, and drilling the two bridge arcs gives the annular product diagram of the disk-open-book binding exterior. [construct]

1.15 **What this does and does not admit.** No repaired supplier was reread, revalidated or hashed for this construction. No canonical definition, statement, coefficients, manifold scope, metadata, gate or workflow control was changed. [construct]

2.1 New topological authoring segment, 2026-10-20. Compose this with the binding/bridge construction. The output is an adapted surface diagram of the actual exterior and its actual fiber; no old doubled-page intersections are retained or counted. [construct]

2.2 **Exact geometric problem.** Let $(M,\gamma)$ be the meridionally sutured exterior constructed in the binding donor, and let $S=-F'$ be its carried, cooriented fiber with the sign needed for top Alexander grading. Its boundary crosses each of the two meridional sutures once. In particular its single boundary component has a nonempty arc on each of $R_+$ and $R_-$. The construction below gives a finite balanced diagram $(\Sigma,\alpha,\beta)$ and a quasi-polygon $P\subset\Sigma$, with $\partial P=A\cup B$, such that $\alpha\cap B=\beta\cap A=\varnothing$ and the rounded surface [construct]

2.3 $$P\times\{1/2\}\ \cup\ A\times[1/2,1]\ \cup\ B\times[0,1/2]$$ [construct]

2.4 is equivalent to the actual marked $S$ through decomposing surfaces. The vertices of $P$ are on $\partial\Sigma$. The construction is allowed to change the diagram and its genus; it retains the exterior, peripheral marking and fiber isotopy class. [construct]

2.5 **Construct the middle polygon and its creases.** Straighten the two meridional boundary annuli as products of their core circle and a height interval, with height increasing from $R_-$ to $R_+$. Along the longitude $\partial S$, the two crossing arcs are vertical in these annuli. Choose a narrow collar of $\partial S$ inside $S$. For the arc of $\partial S$ lying on the positive side, join its two suture-crossing points by an interior parallel arc; the region between the original arc and this parallel arc is a boundary bigon $D_+$. Do the same on the negative side, giving $D_-$. Retain the endpoints at the two actual suture crossings. The remainder $P$ has one edge $A$ adjacent to $D_+$ and one edge $B$ adjacent to $D_-$. Its vertices are those crossing points, and its orientation is the given orientation of $S$. [construct]

2.6 Give $P$ constant function value $c=1/2$. Parametrize $D_+$ by an interval across its collar so the function increases from $c$ at $A$ to $1$ at $R_+$, matching the already specified boundary height on the sides. On $D_-$ it increases from $0$ at $R_-$ to $c$ at $B$. At $A$ crease the surface so its positive middle normal points toward $D_+$, and at $B$ crease it in the opposite direction. These are the two local graph models of an oriented right-angle crease. On a small normal neighborhood of each bigon extend the function constantly in that normal coordinate; near $P$ extend it by $c+\varepsilon n$, where $n$ is its positive normal coordinate. The crease choices make these extensions agree on their overlaps, after using smaller collar rectangles and a monotone interpolation. In particular the gradient is nonzero there and has the specified coorientation through the middle polygon. [construct]

2.7 Extend this locally defined function, together with the sutured boundary heights, over the remaining compact manifold. Use any finite relative smooth handle presentation to obtain a Morse extension, taking perturbations supported outside the prescribed neighborhood. Such a presentation can be obtained from a finite relative triangulation by thickening its simplices in increasing dimension; rounding their collars supplies the local Morse handle charts. All choices here are finite. Call the resulting function $f_0$. [construct]

2.8 **Reorder handles and remove the unwanted polygon feet.** Reorder the relative handles so index-one critical values lie below $c$ and index-two values above it. At the middle level this has the following explicit effect. Every index-one handle moved from above $c$ inserts a tube into that level, whose belt circle is an alpha curve. Every index-two handle moved from below $c$ inserts a tube with beta belt circle, as seen by reversing the handle chart. Minima and maxima crossing the middle add separate spherical level components. The actual surface $S$ is not discarded: intersect it with the new middle level, retaining the boundary bands. Its middle part $P'$ can acquire holes at the tube feet. The additional alpha belt circles themselves miss $P'$, and similarly for additional beta belt circles. [construct]

2.9 The following finite removal performs the required geometric repair. On each component of $P'$ choose a finite rooted tree from its nonempty $A$ edge meeting every component of its intersection with the old alpha circles. Push parallel alpha fingers along this tree to the root. After this, every alpha portion meeting $P'$ has an endpoint on $A$, with no closed alpha component confined to $P'$. The fingers are parallel inside narrow tree ribbons, so alpha circles remain mutually disjoint and miss $B$. Use a tree rooted on $B$ for beta circles. Its beta fingers likewise remain disjoint and miss $A$. In particular every component of $P'\setminus\bigcup\beta$ meets $B$: the beta arcs have both endpoints on $B$, and no beta circle remains in the interior. The corresponding statement holds with alpha and $A$ exchanged. [construct]

2.10 For a foot of an additional alpha-belt tube, choose an arc from that foot to $B$ inside $P'\setminus\bigcup\beta$. First slide every old alpha curve crossing this arc over the tube's alpha belt circle, using parallel copies of that arc. This clears the chosen corridor and preserves the complete disk systems. Then push the $B$ edge through the corridor and across the tube foot. In the actual manifold this last push is an isotopy of the negative boundary band of $S$: follow its negative gradient collar through the tube chart. Thus the surface remains equivalent as a decomposing surface, and the foot ceases to be a boundary component of its middle polygon. The push creates no beta intersection because the corridor misses beta. For a beta-belt foot, use the symmetric corridor to $A$, clear crossing beta curves by beta disk slides, and push the positive boundary band. Each operation removes one unwanted foot. There are finitely many, so the procedure terminates. [construct]

2.11 After this removal the middle polygon misses all auxiliary tubes introduced by handle reordering. Remove index-zero handles by a rooted spanning tree of the one-handle incidence graph, rooted at the nonempty incoming boundary; cancel each terminal zero/one pair in its actual handle chart. The manifold is connected to that incoming boundary, so such a tree reaches every zero handle. Use the dual rooted tree from the outgoing boundary to remove index-three handles with two-handles. The polygon and its boundary bands miss the auxiliary tube neighborhoods just cleared, so these cancellations can be made away from them. The remaining middle level and attaching circles give a relative diagram with only index-one and index-two handles. [construct]

2.12 Its two compressed boundary surfaces are exactly the original $R_-$ and $R_+$, and no closed compressed component remains. Since $\chi(R_-)=\chi(R_+)$, the two numbers of handles agree. Every component of either cut attaching surface meets the sutured boundary, so the diagram is balanced. By construction alpha misses $B$, beta misses $A$, and the rounded middle polygon with its bands is the original marked $S$ up to the explicit band isotopies. This gives the asserted surface diagram. [construct]

2.13 **What the cut represents.** Replace $P$ by the two copies $P_A,P_B$, retaining alpha only on $P_A$ and beta only on $P_B$. This is the literal diagrammatic cut along the rounded surface just constructed: below the middle level use the $P_A$ sheet, above it use $P_B$, and on the boundary bands use the same collar-height coordinate. Since $S$ is the carried fiber, the resulting sutured manifold is the marked product already supplied in the binding donor. [construct]

2.14 This is a topological identification of the cut manifold. It does not identify its possibly nonempty attaching-curve diagram with the empty product diagram by signed chain maps. Nor does it make the diagram admissible, make it nice, classify its disk counts, construct coherent integral orientations, or prove the product computation is invariant. Those are still actual analytic and move operations. In particular no new claim of one outer generator follows from this construction. [construct] ∎

## Statement

A good admissible surface-adapted balanced diagram can be made nice by a finite sequence of permissible fingers and own-family disk slides preserving its surface marking. Weak admissibility is preserved. Every complementary region of the underlying diagram disjoint from its true boundary is a bigon or square.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-sutured-floer-chain-complex]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F2] [[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F3] [[lem-marked-fiber-admits-a-sutured-surface-diagram]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

## Proof

**Given:** The actual diagrams, markings, orientation classes, and admissibility hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Let (Σ,α,β,P) be the actual good adapted diagram, with ∂P=A∪B, whose A and B components are arcs ending on ∂Σ. Put 𝒜=α∪B and ℬ=β∪A. Permissible α fingers and slides avoid B; permissible β fingers and slides avoid A. Thus they carry the actual surface and its specified boundary marking. Corners of P are kept fixed. [construct]

1.2 **The finite geometric operation.** First remove nondisk complementary regions. The quantity [construct]

1.3 a = Σ_R (1−χ(R)) [construct]

1.4 is taken over regions of Σ\(𝒜∪ℬ). A nondisk region admits a proper nonseparating arc δ with one endpoint on an α edge and the other on ℬ, or with the two colors interchanged. Here is the obstruction to the contrary: a component whose frontier has no such α edge has frontier in B and ℬ; alternating endpoints at the vertices of P then force a whole boundary component in A or B, or a linear relation among the complete α or β attaching circles modulo ∂Σ. The first is excluded by goodness; the second by the compressionbody disk-system condition. Cut a nonseparating arc initially with any endpoints and slide its ends along the frontier until one of these permissible pairs is reached. A finger of the selected attaching circle along δ replaces R by a region of Euler characteristic χ(R)+1 and an extra bigon. Consequently a decreases by one. All other components have unchanged Euler characteristic. There are finitely many regions, and a is a nonnegative integer, so this stage ends. [construct]

1.5 For a disk region with 2n corners let b(R)=max(n−2,0). Regions meeting ∂Σ need not be improved. The distance of a region is the least number of α/β crossings of a path from ∂Σ avoiding A∪B. A path can be moved off vertices; passage through a vertex counts two crossings. Every region has finite distance: otherwise a component cut off from ∂Σ by A∪B would have a closed A or B frontier. Let d be the largest distance of a bad region. At distance d sort the positive badnesses b₁≥…≥b_m and order the complexity [construct]

1.6 (Σ b_i, −b₁,…,−b_m) [construct]

1.7 lexicographically, padding with zeros if necessary. This is well founded: the first coordinate is a nonnegative integer and, at fixed first coordinate, the sorted lists are finite in number. [construct]

1.8 Choose the last, smallest bad region D_m, and a β side b* adjacent to a region D* of distance d−1; interchange α and β if required. Label its 𝒜 sides a₁,…,a_n beginning after b*. Starting through any a_i, continue straight through opposite sides of squares of distance at least d. A corridor stops at a bigon, a smaller-distance region, a bad region, or a return to D_m. At least one corridor escapes D_m. If all returned, the union of the return strips has frontier a nonempty integral sum of β circles and arcs in A. Since A has no circle components and its vertices lie on ∂Σ, this gives a forbidden relation among the β disks modulo the boundary. No completeness assumption about a closed surface is involved. [construct]

1.9 The following are the actual replacements; they stay in the listed corridors and avoid A. [construct]

1.10 * If an escaping corridor starts at a_i with 2≤i≤n−1, push b* through that corridor. The intermediate squares are each subdivided into three squares. D_m splits into two regions with total badness b(D_m)−1. If the terminal region is a bigon or has smaller distance, the first complexity coordinate decreases. If it is a different distance-d bad region, that region absorbs one unit of badness. The total is unchanged, but an earlier entry in the descending list increases, so the negative sorted list decreases. * Suppose only an end corridor escapes, relabeling so a₁ escapes. If n=3, the corridor from a₂ returns through a₃ and contains a complete β circle: its other possible boundary, a closed A component, is excluded. Slide b* over that β circle along the corridor. D_m becomes a bigon and a square. Extra badness is deposited in D*, whose distance is smaller. * If n>3 and the corridor from a₂ returns at a_l with l<n, use its reverse from a_l to a₂, then continue out a₁ to the escaping corridor. The finger cuts off two squares and two remaining bad pieces whose total badness is b(D_m)−1. * If that corridor returns at a_n, use the return corridor from a_{n−1}; its other end a_p satisfies 2<p<n−1. Follow its reverse from a_p to a_{n−1}, then the first return corridor backwards from a_n to a₂, then escape through a₁. This cuts off four squares and leaves two pieces with total badness b(D_m)−1. The interiors of these square corridors are disjoint: a shared opposite-side continuation would identify their starting and returning sides, contrary to the specified distinct indices. Thus the indicated finger is embedded after taking parallel tracks. [construct]

1.11 No replacement increases the maximum distance of a bad region. The distance-d complexity decreases. Eventually distance d has no bad regions; then d decreases. This gives a finite word of permissible fingers and disk slides, with the actual surface P carried at every step. [construct]

1.12 **Admissibility is preserved, rather than reasserted.** The elementary coefficient calculation is local and does not use genus, a closed cap, or coefficient field. Subdivide a long finger into elementary passages past a crossing. In the passage label the three old regions D₁,D₂,D₃ and the five new pieces D′₁,…,D′₅ by following the old region germs. For a periodic domain with coefficients c_i on the new pieces, constancy of its boundary jump along the same attaching circle gives [construct]

1.13 c₂−c₁ = c₄−c₃ = c₂−c₅, c₁−c₃ = c₂−c₄ = c₅−c₃. [construct]

1.14 Thus c₅=c₁ and c₄=c₂+c₃−c₁. Erasing the finger gives the old periodic domain with coefficients c₁,c₂,c₃. Each of these old coefficients still occurs on an actual new region; coefficients outside the small passage are unchanged. A new nonzero domain cannot erase to zero, since these equations would then make every new coefficient zero. Hence both signs of every old nonzero periodic domain survive, and there is no new positive periodic domain. [construct]

1.15 For the corridor slide, write c* for the coefficient of D*, c₁,c₂ for the two D_m pieces, and c_{i,1},c_{i,2} for the two sides of the i-th corridor square. The jump equations along the sliding β circle and the circle slid over are [construct]

1.16 c₁−c* = c_{i,1}−c_{i,2} = c₂−c*  for every i. [construct]

1.17 In particular c₁=c₂. Erasing the slide gives the old periodic coefficients c*, c₁, c_{i,1}, with all untouched coefficients unchanged. Again every selected coefficient is retained on an actual new region; if the erased domain is zero the displayed equations force all coefficients zero. Both signs survive. These equations also apply to the band slides in the nondisk reduction, after separating the band into local passages. Along A or B no jump is allowed except the existing surface edge; the operation avoids the forbidden color, so the same calculation applies there. [construct]

1.18 Consequently the finite permissible word preserves weak admissibility without moving the boundary marking or replacing the actual periodic-domain lattice by closed-surface homology. [construct]

1.19 **The underlying diagram is nice.** The surface algorithm makes every region disjoint from ∂Σ in Σ\(α∪β∪A∪B) a bigon or square. Erasing A and B glues these pieces across surface edges. A resulting region disjoint from ∂Σ has nonnegative Euler measure. Its alternating α/β boundary therefore makes it a bigon, a square, or a corner-free disk or annulus. A corner-free disk or annulus has frontier a sum of whole attaching circles; its coefficient-one domain is a nonzero nonnegative periodic domain. Admissibility excludes it. Thus every region of the underlying actual sutured diagram which can occur in a counted domain is a bigon or square. [construct] ∎
