## Statement

Two balanced Heegaard diagrams of the same marked sutured manifold are connected by relative attaching-circle isotopies, own-family disk slides, and ordinary stabilizations and destabilizations. An ordinary stabilization can be moved by such slides to the true boundary region. Under the Axiom of Choice, these moves induce integral chain homotopy equivalences for the transported coherent orientation class, and the product sutured manifold has integral homology equal to one copy of the integers. For supplied actual coherent systems on a homology-product branch, the periodic-domain character ambiguity vanishes.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. It is assumed when invoking existence, regularity, compactification, and invariant comparison maps from the imported integral sutured analytic framework. The finite domain and determinant calculations retain their stated conditional supplied-data hypotheses; no unconditional Countable-Choice analytic existence theorem is asserted. In particular the Countable-Choice selection result applies only GIVEN its actual pointwise operator constructions, not merely because the diagrams or domain classes are countable.

[F1] [[lem-integral-sutured-floer-compactness-and-orientations]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F2] [[lem-integral-sutured-auxiliary-triangle-and-move-maps]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F3] [[def-sutured-floer-chain-complex]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

[F4] [[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region]] supplies its stated definitions or proved operator/construction interface at its stated scope.

## Proof

**Given:** The actual diagrams, markings, orientation classes, and admissibility hypotheses in the statement. The Axiom of Choice is assumed for the analytic invocations [A1]; the relative finite-move geometry and supplied finite-complex algebra keep their stated inputs.

1.1 New construction, 2026-10-20. Both negative and positive marked boundary surfaces are assumed connected, as they are for the knot cut along its connected Seifert surface. Their genus is arbitrary. All boundary identifications and sutured collars are held fixed. This does not apply a closed Reidemeister--Singer conclusion to a manifold with boundary. [construct]

1.2 **1. Translate the actual diagrams into relative handles.** A balanced sutured diagram with connected compressed boundary surfaces gives a relative Morse presentation: start with $R_-\times[0,1]$, attach its $d$ one-handles with the actual alpha co-core disks, then its $d$ beta two-handles, ending at the specified $R_+$. The vertical annuli are the fixed sutured collar, not additional capped surfaces. Its middle surface and disk boundaries are the original diagram. The reverse construction takes a relative self-indexed Morse function with only index-one and index-two critical points and reads the same compressionbodies. The handle charts and their product collars provide both constructions explicitly. [construct]

1.3 Take the two such presentations to be compared. Their boundary height functions and collar gradients agree after collar rescaling. Join their interior functions and pseudo-gradients through smooth families fixed in that collar. Make the family generic in the following relative sense. Away from the boundary, transverse jets make the critical locus a compact one-manifold except at finitely many ordinary birth/death points. The local exceptional model is [construct]

1.4 $$f_\tau=x_1^3-\tau x_1\ \pm x_2^2\ \pm x_3^2+\text{constant}.$$ [construct]

1.5 Higher critical degeneracies impose at least two independent jet conditions and are avoided by a one-parameter perturbation. Critical-value crossings are transverse and finite. Choose the pseudo-gradients Morse--Smale except at isolated transverse same-index connecting trajectories. Their zero-dimensional parameterized connecting spaces are compact: a broken trajectory would have strictly decreasing intermediate indices and cannot begin and end at the same index; the fixed local birth charts are removed and treated separately. Thus there are finitely many handle-slide times. Perturbations and the fixed birth charts are supported away from the protected boundary collar. This constructs a finite relative Cerf word, rather than inferring one from a closed double. [construct]

1.6 For each regular parameter put all index-one handles below the middle level and all index-two handles above it by reordering along the chosen pseudo-gradient. Morse--Smale trajectories cannot run from an index-one critical point to an index-two critical point in the descending direction, so this reordering introduces no new attaching intersection. Smooth reordering between exceptional times transports the middle level and its disk systems by isotopy. A same-index connecting trajectory changes the corresponding attaching disk by a band sum with the other disk along that trajectory's small flow tube. This is precisely an alpha disk slide or a beta disk slide, according to index. Its band lies on the actual middle surface and misses the other disks in that same family. The fixed boundary collar remains untouched. [construct]

1.7 **2. Eliminate the auxiliary zero/three handles by actual forest moves.** During the family allow minima and maxima; they must not be confused with stabilizations. The union of the incoming product collar, zero-handle balls and one-handle tubes is a regular neighborhood of a finite graph rooted on $R_-$. That graph is connected to the root: a two-handle attaches along a circle in one existing component, and a three-handle cannot connect components, so a component missing the root could not be joined later to the connected $M$. [construct]

1.8 Choose a rooted spanning tree. Starting at its terminal vertices, absorb each zero-handle ball and its tree tube into its parent ball or the incoming collar. Each absorption is the explicit standard ball-plus-tube chart, fixed outside that neighborhood. The remaining non-tree edges are the relative one-handles. Thus this operation presents the **same embedded compressionbody**, with the same positive boundary, using no minima. The dual operation from $R_+$ eliminates maxima and their tree two-handles. [construct]

1.9 Different spanning trees change only the complete disk presentation, by actual disk slides. It suffices to treat a tree exchange $T'=T-e+f$. The edge $f$ creates one circuit with the old tree. Slide the endpoints of the finitely many non-tree edges incident to the subtree below $e$ along the circuit through $f$, using parallel narrow bands. Then $f$ is the tree tube and $e$ the remaining non-tree tube. In the regular graph neighborhood these are literal one-handle core slides; dualizing them gives disk slides of the corresponding co-cores. Inverting an edge orientation or relabelling a disk changes no surface. Every pair of finite spanning trees is connected by these exchanges, since an edge of $T'\setminus T$ removes an edge outside $T'$ from its unique circuit. Hence the forest choices require no unproved comparison of arbitrary compressionbody disk systems. [construct]

1.10 An index-zero/one birth is an extra ball attached by a tree tube. Its absorption is an isotopy of the positive boundary, with no genus change. The dual index-two/three birth has the same property. An index-one/two birth adds one tube to each side whose two new co-core boundaries meet once in its actual birth ball. It is an ordinary Heegaard stabilization. The remaining regular and exceptional changes are the isotopies and disk slides described above. At both endpoints the forest is empty and the prescribed original diagrams are retained, up to precisely those forest disk slides. This gives a finite relative word of isotopies, alpha/beta disk slides, stabilizations and their inverses, fixing the entire marked sutured boundary. [construct]

1.11 **3. Move a stabilization to a genuine zero boundary region.** The finite relative word may place its stabilization disk in a region that does not meet the sutured boundary. An analytic product argument cannot assume that region has zero domain. The following topological conversion uses the stabilization handle itself to correct that location. [construct]

1.12 Let $D$ be its old-surface disk and choose another disk $E$ in an actual boundary region of the **original** diagram. A surface isotopy fixed on $\partial\Sigma$ carries $D$ to $E$; extend its vector field into a two-sided collar of the splitting surface. This transports the stabilized splitting and both compressionbodies. It produces the stabilization at $E$ of the **transported** attaching systems, which need not have $E$ in a boundary region. Do not apply an analytic stabilization map at that intermediate diagram. [construct]

1.13 Undo the old attaching-system isotopy while keeping the new punctured torus at $E$. There is a finite lift using own-family slides over the new co-core. Choose the center of $E$ to be a regular value of the finite isotopy traces of all old circles. Its preimage in those compact traces is finite. Away from these crossings the isotopy lifts unchanged to the surface with the new punctured torus. At one crossing, compress that punctured torus along its new alpha circle if the moving family is alpha. The local picture is a disk with the two marked alpha cap faces. The desired old-arc sweep across that disk lifts by detouring across each cap face it meets. Each detour is one band sum with the new alpha circle, with the two faces carrying opposite orientations. After these at most two detours, the remaining arc sweep is an isotopy in the punctured disk. All bands lie in a small parallel corridor of the swept arc and avoid the other alpha curves. This is an actual pair of alpha disk slides, not a point-push asserted to be trivial. For a beta crossing compress along the new beta circle and use beta slides instead. Factor simultaneous circle-family isotopies into these finitely many single crossings. [construct]

1.14 The resulting finite slide/isotopy word returns the old attaching systems to their original positions while the new torus remains at $E$. The endpoint is now the standard stabilization of the original diagram in a genuine zero boundary region. Reversing the word relates it to the initially located stabilization. This avoids an incidence-neck stabilization claim at a region of possibly positive multiplicity. It also avoids treating an ambiently transported nonboundary region as though it became a boundary region. [construct]

1.15 **4. The boundary-region stabilization has actual signed inverse maps.** In the disk $E$ attach the standard punctured torus with circles $a_0,b_0$ meeting once at $c$, disjoint from all old circles. The new generator set is exactly $\{x\times c\}$. The old boundary region remains connected through the new torus complement and its joining collar. Every sutured disk domain has zero coefficient in that whole region, hence has zero multiplicity in the new torus and the joining corridor. This is the required actual zero-region calculation. [construct]

1.16 Choose split almost complex data on the configuration neighborhood with one coordinate near $c$ and the remaining coordinates on the old side of that zero corridor. Its divisor barriers are the same as in the signed exterior construction. Any counted strip has the new coordinate constantly $c$ and the old coordinates equal to an old counted strip: a nonconstant sheet entering the new torus or crossing the zero corridor would have positive degree in a zero region. Conversely every old strip times $c$ is a new one. The actual linearized operator is its old operator plus the invertible constant transverse strip operator at $c$. The latter has its canonical positive determinant orientation. Thus counts and signs agree, regularity is preserved, and [construct]

1.17 $$I(x)=x\times c,\qquad P(x\times c)=x$$ [construct]

1.18 are inverse integer chain isomorphisms, with zero inverse homotopies, for these actual split choices. Arbitrary chosen strip data on that stabilized diagram align with the split choices by the actual signed continuation construction, including the constant-generator regularity argument; no additional generator-jet agreement is assumed. [construct]

1.19 On the homology-product branch every diagram in the relative word is still a diagram of the same marked homology product. Its relative handle complex is integrally acyclic, so its alpha/beta intersection matrix is unimodular and its periodic-domain lattice is zero. Hence the signed local slide, isotopy, choice-alignment and boundary-region stabilization operations already constructed apply in that word. All auxiliaries can be prepared with their actual zero-area periodic forms; their compatible determinant and top-unit constructions retain the full boundary radical. Composing the actual maps and their explicit reverse homotopies gives a signed chain equivalence between the two original marked diagrams. For the product manifold the endpoint may be its empty product diagram, so this comparison identifies its actual integer homology with $\mathbb Z$. [construct]

## Proof

**Given:** The actual marked sutured diagrams and decomposition hypotheses of the statement, with a specified coherent orientation class. The Axiom of Choice is assumed for the analytic invocations [A1]; the relative finite-move geometry and supplied finite-complex algebra keep their stated inputs.

1.1 **Product one-handles are literal complex identifications.** Adding a product one-handle with feet at sutures attaches a two-dimensional band to the boundary of the actual Heegaard surface and adds no attaching circle. The resulting handlebody thickening is exactly the three-dimensional product one-handle: the two level faces are its upper and lower rectangles and its remaining face carries the suture. The band lies in a true boundary region. Every counted domain has coefficient zero there. Point-divisor positivity therefore prevents a holomorphic trace from entering the band, not merely from passing through its center. The generator set, disk maps, linearized operators and determinant orientations are consequently unchanged. A periodic domain is also unchanged, because its coefficient on the new band is zero and its attaching-circle boundary is the old one. This gives a literal integral chain identification, with the specified orientation character. Cutting a product disk is the inverse operation. In particular finitely many such handles may connect suture components without changing the complex. [construct]

1.2 **An actual closure diagram for any connected R₊ and R₋.** First suppose the suture has one component; write g for the genus of R₊. A self-indexing relative Morse function on M has r index-one and r index-two points after the relative zero/three cancellations. Its middle surface F̃ has genus g+r. Choose a small disk D₊ near the boundary and an arc δ₊ from it to the boundary disjoint from the finitely many exceptional flow points; follow them through the regular flow corridor to obtain D̃,δ̃,D₋,δ₋. Choose the closing diffeomorphism ψ:R₊→R₋ to match these collars. Gluing by ψ and filling the resulting boundary torus with meridian equal to the joined cut meridians constructs an actual closed Y and core knot K; the glued level face is its Seifert surface and cutting it recovers M with its marking. [construct]

1.3 Put A₊=R₊\intD₊ and Ã=F̃\intD̃. Choose 2g independent disjoint ξ₋ arcs with endpoints on the old boundary, avoiding δ₋ and the exceptional points; carry them to Ã and to A₊ by flow and ψ. Choose 2g independent disjoint η₊ arcs with endpoints on ∂D₊, avoiding δ₊ and the exceptional points; flow them to Ã. Glue A₊ to Ã with the two flow annuli, one over ∂D₊ and one over the old boundary. Double each ξ and η across its annulus. Add the r lower and r upper critical circles, the circle α₁=∂D̃, and the meridian μ=δ₊∪δ̃ with its two annular joining arcs. Choose w,z on opposite sides of μ next to its crossing with the old boundary longitude λ. [construct]

1.4 This is a complete genus-(2g+1+r) Heegaard diagram of the actual closure. The lower ξ disks are the flow rectangles from R₋ to the middle level joined through the ψ identification; the critical α disks are the actual lower co-cores and α₁ is the D-flow tube co-core. 1.5 The local meridional Chern calculation identifies its top generators with the outer set, and the full signed cut operation identifies this top complex with SFC(M). It is legitimate here with nonzero periodic domains: use the pullback of the specified orientation character as in the new separating-cut operation. More generally the disk-lift argument for the nice adapted closure uses precisely that same pullback calculation; it does not require a zero-periodic cut. Different closure maps and fillings compare through the actual M complex, so no separate closed-manifold gluing-independence assertion is assumed. Multiple sutures are treated by the literal product-handle operation just proved; no link knotification theorem is needed. [construct]

1.6 **The essential once-punctured-torus attachment.** Suppose M is obtained from M₂ by gluing the vertical boundary of G×I to a product annulus a⊂∂M₂, where G is a once-punctured torus; the remaining sutures are outside this product region. Use the closure diagram just constructed. On the middle surface of M₂ write B̃=F̃₂\intD̃ and denote its other boundary component by ã; the old boundary is λ̃. Choose σ̃ from λ̃ to ã disjoint from the α circles and δ̃, and τ̃ from ∂D̃ to ã disjoint from the β circles and δ̃. [construct]

1.7 Here are the actual allowed stabilizations of these arcs. At a crossing to be removed, puncture two tiny disks on opposite sides of σ̃, join their boundary circles by a tube, put a new α belt circle round one foot and a new β longitude through the tube. Redirect each old crossing strand through the tube on a separate track, using own-family slides over that longitude. The old arc σ̃ stays on the old surface and misses the new belt; it crosses the new longitude once. Multiple strands use parallel tracks. The same tunnel redirects a crossing of τ̃. Repeat for the finite crossing list. The color-reversed operation on τ̃ then makes it miss the ξ arcs and intersect one stabilization α circle once. The result has σ̃∩τ̃=∅; σ̃ meets precisely one β circle b, and τ̃ precisely one α circle a₀. All operations occur away from δ̃ and the closing marks. They are the actual relative stabilizations already covered by the signed move word. [construct]

1.8 Choose the remaining ξ arcs on the lower level avoiding σ and δ, and the η arcs on the upper level avoiding τ and δ. A slide over b removes any remaining η–σ intersection. On G choose two disjoint ξ arcs and two disjoint η arcs with ξ_i·η_j=δ_ij and no other intersections. Obtain them from the standard square presentation of a punctured torus by taking the two cut co-cores and their small transverse translates; their complement is a disk. Extend ξ₂,ξ₃ to the λ boundary along four parallel σ tracks, and η₂,η₃ to the D boundary along four parallel τ tracks. Use the same extension on the upper level and then the closure construction. There are two distinguished middle intersections x₂,x₃, one in each ξ_iη_i pair. [construct]

1.9 The β circle b now crosses the two ξ tracks twice each. Slide b twice over β₂ with opposite orientations, and twice over β₃ with opposite orientations. Each pair eliminates its two ξ crossings and has zero total homology change. Route the resulting circle outside G by the intervening annular isotopy. Call it b*. It is homologous to b, and its upper-level restriction b*∩A₊ is relatively null-homologous. Its two crossings with a₀ are called x,y. The region between their a₀ and b* boundary arcs contains the two G bands; it is an embedded genus-one region Q with exactly these two convex corners. It is obtained from a disk strip by attaching its two bands in alternating endpoint order. This description specifies its topology and edges without depending on the schematic picture. [construct]

1.10 **Exhaust the possible disks in this actual block.** Apply the uniform relative windings on the upper ξ arcs and the middle α circles other than a₀. The geometric duals are obtained by cutting the lower ξ system: the remaining middle surface is connected (it is a punctured lower face with finitely many extra disk holes), so its dual paths can avoid σ,τ,δ. The basis vector for a₀ is reserved. For a nonnegative whole periodic domain, winding removes the other α coefficients. The meridian μ has only the α₁ crossing, so pairing its boundary with μ also removes the α₁ coefficient. On the upper face, independence of the η relative classes and relative null-homology of b* leave only the b* contribution. The untouched stabilization dual β circle intersects a₀ once and misses the other β circles; intersection with it removes that multiple. Independence of the β disk classes then forces zero. This proves actual weak admissibility; it does not claim that all periodic domains vanish. [construct]

1.11 For a differential disk between top generators, the upper restriction is a relative periodic domain because its endpoints lie on the middle side. Winding removes its ξ coefficients. Its coefficient at λ is zero by the μ,α₁,w,z collar equations. Relative η-independence now gives [construct]

1.12 ∂(D∩A₊) modulo ∂A₊ = m(b*∩A₊). [construct]

1.13 The two ξ₂,ξ₃ coordinates are forced to be x₂,x₃, since they have only their own η intersections outside the forbidden upper face. Their α and β boundary jumps vanish: they vanish on the upper ξ and η segments, and a stationary coordinate has constant whole-circle boundary coefficient. The four local coefficients at each of x₂,x₃ are therefore equal; the region joins the zero collar component, so they are all zero. Following these zero strips to a₀ and α₁ gives two zero quadrants at x and two at y. The remaining corner coefficient is m, hence positivity gives m≥0. [construct]

1.14 If m>0, the zero strips separate from the remaining trace a component supported on Q with its two boundary edges on a₀ and b*. Its endpoint boundary is m(y−x). There is only one moving coordinate on a₀, so an actual generator difference has coefficient at most one there; consequently m=1 for this component. Its domain has e(Q)=χ(Q)−2/4=−3/2 and endpoint sum 1/2, hence Maslov index −1. For a regular strip problem this component cannot occur. Equivalently its trace would have degree one over the strip but degree one onto the genus-one region Q, which is impossible after compactifying the strip to a disk. Thus m=0. All disk multiplicities in the attached genus-one block and upper face are zero, and every differential disk is supported in the unchanged middle B̃. [construct]

1.15 **Compare with the literal M₂ diagram.** Attach a rectangle I×[0,1] between the λ̃ and ã boundaries of B̃, with its σ endpoint outside one attaching interval and its τ endpoint inside the other. This is the actual product one-handle on M₂. In the new surface C̃ take ζ₂=I×{1/2}, ζ₃=σ̃. Take ω₂ to be τ̃ followed by a vertical rectangle arc and a parallel δ̃; take ω₃ as the interior frontier of a narrow neighborhood of τ̃∪ã. Double these arcs in the closure as above, replacing only the old two G arc pairs. Slide b over the doubled ω₃ once. The two replacement coordinates y₂,y₃ are then forced, and the remaining generators are exactly the same intersection tuples in B̃ as before. [construct]

1.16 Perform the same protected windings. The upper restriction of a differential domain has boundary a combination of the remaining η arcs and the new b restriction. These relative classes are independent in C₊: cutting ζ₂ across the rectangle and ζ₃ along σ opens the two boundary components, after which the remaining η system cuts the old handles; the b strand crosses the reserved stabilization co-core once. A relation must therefore have every coefficient zero. The λ′ collar and y₂,y₃ quadrants are zero by the same boundary equations. Hence every differential disk is again supported in B̃. Conversely a disk in B̃ extends by the forced stationary coordinates to both diagrams. [construct]

1.17 The map replacing (x₂,x₃) by (y₂,y₃) and keeping the B̃ tuple therefore bijects all differential disks. Choose the complex structures literally equal on B̃ and use the invertible constant factors on the forced coordinates. The linearized operators are conjugate, and so are their finite-kernel determinant splices. Transport the specified orientation character through the common supported domains; any unused periodic characters do not alter this supported differential. Generator signs align the reference orientations. This gives an actual integral chain isomorphism after the admitted signed moves. Thus attachment or removal of this essential genus-one product region preserves the integral chain type with its induced orientation class. [construct]

1.18 **Reduce the full separating annulus to this block.** Let A be a separating product annulus with connected R₊ and R₋ and balanced cuts M₁,M₂. Its boundary components are essential in R(γ), as required for a product-annulus decomposing surface. Form F₊=R₊(γ₁)∪A∪R₋(γ₂), rounded and pushed off the boundary; form F₋ with signs reversed. Euler additivity and balance give χ(F_±)=χ(R₊), and the three-dimensional region between the faces gives their actual relative homology [R₊]. They are horizontal surfaces. Applying the newly constructed horizontal chain operation cuts M into M₁ with a product face of M₂ attached and M₂ with a product face of M₁ attached. Consequently it suffices to remove an attached product region T×I. [construct]

1.19 If that region meets an original suture, choose a cut-arc forest in T rooted at that suture. The rectangles arc×I are product disks. If it meets no original suture, first connect external sutures by literal product one-handles. Essentiality excludes a disk product component. Choose a once-punctured torus G in T, and apply the genus-one block above along ∂G×I. The remainder T\intG is planar after repeating for each genus handle. It now meets the newly exposed sutures, and its rooted cut-arc forest again gives product disks. All these operations are in the actual attached product region and leave the complementary M_i fixed. There are finitely many genus handles and forest edges. [construct]

1.20 Combining the horizontal chain map, the explicit product one-handle/disk identifications, and the essential genus-one supported-domain isomorphism gives the separating-annulus graded tensor chain operation. It gives Ni's stated homology tensor formula over any field and the integral Künneth/Tor formulation. This is a constructed essential-annulus operation; it neither invokes a zero-H₂ annulus theorem on an arbitrary manifold nor supplies characteristic-product or taut-hierarchy geometry. [construct] ∎

## Proof

**Given:** The actual diagrams, markings, orientation classes, and admissibility hypotheses in the statement. The Axiom of Choice is assumed for the analytic invocations [A1]; the relative finite-move geometry and supplied finite-complex algebra keep their stated inputs.

1.1 New construction, 2026-10-20. No canonical source or accepted supplier is changed or rechecked. This file concerns the difference between existing coherent orientations. It does not assume existence, coherence, or signed diagram invariance merely from orientability of individual determinant lines. [construct]

1.2 **1. Derive the actual character group.** Fix a finite transverse balanced sutured diagram $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\alpha,\beta)$ and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^d(\operatorname{int}\Sigma)$. Treat the empty diagram separately: its generator and orientation are canonical. For $d>0$, let $\mathcal G$ be the groupoid of Whitney-disk homotopy classes with its actual generators as objects and splicing as composition. Work separately on each connected component of this groupoid. Fix a base generator $x_0$ and reference paths $\theta_x:x_0\to x$ for its finitely many objects. Let $\Pi=\mathcal G(x_0,x_0)$, and let $\mathcal P$ be the integral periodic-domain group. Both endpoints and the ordered attaching circles are retained throughout. [construct]

1.3 The domain homomorphism $D:\Pi\to\mathcal P$ has kernel exactly the image of sphere insertion. Here is the needed topological proof. The coefficient of $\alpha_i$ in the boundary of a periodic Whitney domain is the winding number of its alpha boundary loop in the $i$th factor of the product torus; the beta coefficients have the same interpretation. This follows by taking a regular point on the relevant attaching circle: its signed boundary preimages count that winding, and are precisely the boundary incidence coefficient of the region chain. If $D(u)=0$, all these windings are zero. Both torus loops are therefore nullhomotopic, since a product of circles has universal cover $\mathbb R^d$. Cap them inside the respective tori; the capped map is a sphere in $X$. Removing the caps expresses the original class as insertion of that sphere into the constant Whitney disk. Conversely, a sphere has zero domain. Indeed its intersection number with $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{d-1}(\Sigma)$ is independent of $p$ along any path in $\operatorname{int}\Sigma$: the moving divisors give the homology between these intersection tests. The union of all coordinates of a compact sphere image is compact in $\operatorname{int}\Sigma$, so choose $p$ in a boundary collar outside it. That intersection number is zero, hence it is zero for every region test point. Thus sphere insertion lies in the kernel. No assertion that $\pi_2(X)=0$ has been made. [construct]

1.4 Write $\Lambda=D(\Pi)\subseteq\mathcal P$. Suppose $o,o'$ are coherent orientation systems, with the same determinant-splicing convention and the canonical complex orientation for sphere insertions. Their ratio $r(u)\in\{\pm1\}$ is constant on each disk class, multiplicative under splicing, and one on sphere insertions. Therefore its restriction to $\Pi$ factors through a unique character $\chi:\Lambda\to\{\pm1\}$. Put $\sigma(x)=r(\theta_x)$. For $u:x\to y$, the class $\theta_x*u*\theta_y^{-1}$ is periodic at $x_0$, and multiplicativity gives the exact formula [construct]

1.5 $$r(u)=\sigma(x)\sigma(y)\,\chi\bigl(D(\theta_x)+D(u)-D(\theta_y)\bigr).$$ [construct]

1.6 Conversely every character of $\Lambda$ produces a coherent twist by this formula: the two reference-domain terms at an intermediate endpoint cancel under composition, and sphere insertions have zero domain. Thus, **if at least one coherent system exists**, their equivalence classes modulo generator sign changes are a torsor for $\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda,\mathbb Z/2)$. This is the exact group justified here. It is not silently replaced by $\operatorname{Hom}(H_2(M),\mathbb Z/2)$ or by all of $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal P,\mathbb Z/2)$; surjectivity of disk classes onto periodic domains has not been assumed. Different connected components of the disk groupoid carry their own such groups. [construct]

1.7 **2. On the rank-one homology-product branch the domain group vanishes.** Use the actual sutured intersection matrix $I$ in the preceding homology-product donor. Its proof derives $\det I=\pm1$ from an actual integral complex with homology $\mathbb Z$, without an $S^3$ normalization. Let $Q$ be any periodic domain, with [construct]

1.8 $$\partial Q=\sum_i a_i\alpha_i+\sum_j b_j\beta_j.$$ [construct]

1.9 Intersect this homologically zero boundary with each $\alpha_i$. The alpha curves are mutually disjoint, so $I b=0$ up to the fixed overall intersection convention. The integer inverse of $I$ gives $b=0$. Hence $\partial Q$ is supported on alpha curves alone. Its coefficient function is constant on each component of $\Sigma\setminus\bigcup\alpha$. Every such component meets $\partial\Sigma$ by the balanced condition, and the coefficient there is zero by the sutured-domain condition. Therefore $Q=0$. This proves $\mathcal P=0$, and hence $\Lambda=0$ in every generator component. [construct]

1.10 It follows that any two **existing** coherent systems on this branch differ only by generator signs. The map $x\mapsto\sigma(x)x$ identifies their actual integer differential matrices: for an index-one class from $x$ to $y$ its count changes by exactly $\sigma(x)\sigma(y)$. This eliminates orientation-character ambiguity on precisely the homology-product branch required by Ni. It does not construct the first coherent system, signed continuation maps, or signed surface-decomposition maps. Nor does it justify using this conclusion before the top-group/decomposition comparison has put the actual cut-manifold complex on that branch. [construct]

1.11 **3. Explicit ambiguity away from that branch.** Take a flat torus $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$, let $\alpha$ be $y=0$, and let $\beta$ be $y=\varepsilon\sin(2\pi x)$, with $0<\varepsilon<1/10$. Remove a small open disk centered near $(1/4,1/2)$, disjoint from the two curves and their thin bigons. The resulting once-punctured torus is a balanced sutured diagram: each nonseparating attaching curve has connected complement meeting the boundary. There are two transverse generators, call them $x,y$, and two embedded empty bigons $B_1,B_2$ from $x$ to $y$. The complement of these thin bigons is the single region meeting the puncture. [construct]

1.12 The periodic-domain group is $\mathbb Z(B_1-B_2)$. To see this directly, its puncture-region coefficient is zero. At either crossing the absence of boundary endpoints forces the two thin coefficients to be opposite. These are the only two remaining coefficients, and every such opposite pair has boundary a sum of the full alpha and beta curves. In particular the diagram is admissible. Every positive disk domain from $x$ to $y$ is $B_1+n(B_2-B_1)$, and nonnegativity forces $n=0$ or $1$. For the reverse endpoint order the analogous coefficients cannot both be nonnegative. With the integrable surface structure each bigon is a single translation class of regular holomorphic strips: a conformal map from the standard strip onto the open Jordan bigon is unique up to translation, and the linearized scalar boundary problem has its one translation kernel and zero cokernel. Thus these are exactly the two differential contributions. [construct]

1.13 Here the nontrivial periodic class is actually realized by $B_1*B_2^{-1}$, so $\Lambda=\mathcal P=\mathbb Z$. Given any coherent orientation system, write the two signed strip counts as $s_1,s_2\in\{\pm1\}$. Its complex is $\partial x=(s_1+s_2)y$, $\partial y=0$. Twist it by $(-1)^{n_p(u)}$, for a test point $p$ in the interior of $B_1$. Domain multiplicity is additive under splicing and zero on spheres, so this is a coherent orientation twist. It changes $s_1$ to $-s_1$ and leaves $s_2$ unchanged. Exactly one of the two coefficients $s_1+s_2$ and $-s_1+s_2$ is zero, and the other is $+2$ or $-2$. The two resulting homologies are therefore $\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z/2$, respectively. They cannot be isomorphic. [construct]

1.14 For existence in this specific example, no free-abelian commutator compatibility is needed: the periodic group is infinite cyclic, the surface has no sphere classes, and the determinant lines of individual strip components are orientable. Choose an orientation for its periodic generator and one reference disk. This is the new differential exhaustion required by that identification; it does not provide the separate taut hierarchy or characteristic-product argument. [construct]

2.1 **Uniform relative winding, not a domain-dependent choice.** Let R be a compact surface with a nonempty prescribed set of zero-multiplicity test points. Write its curve set as Ξ∪Θ, with Ξ={ξ₁,…,ξ_n}. Assume circles τ_i are algebraically dual to Ξ, geometrically meeting their own ξ_i once, and that those intersections lie in a connected open U containing a zero test point and disjoint from Θ. All winding corridors avoid the protected boundary marks. Over Q let X and Y be the spans of Ξ and Θ, and let K be the kernel of X⊕Y→H₁(R,∂R;Q), with the zero test-point normalization. A relative periodic domain is uniquely determined by its boundary in K: the difference of two fillings is constant on R and its value is fixed to zero at the test point. [construct]

2.2 Put X₀=proj_X K. Row-reduce a basis so ζ_i=ξ_i+Σ_{j>m}a_ij ξ_j, i=1,…,m, and choose a relative domain Q_i filling ζ_i plus a Θ-chain. A domain with zero Ξ-boundary is zero on U: its boundary misses U, so its coefficient is constant there and vanishes at the test point. This kernel fact is the required control of arbitrarily large Θ-components; a bound depending only on the Ξ-coefficients would otherwise be invalid. [construct]

2.3 Wind simultaneously along τ_i and a parallel oppositely oriented copy. Along one turn the successive strip coefficients differ by the ξ_i boundary coefficient. Therefore at the two exit ports the coefficient on Q_i is increased and decreased by the number of turns. Put those ports in U outside all other winding annuli. The off-diagonal coefficients of Q_j at these ports, j≠i, remain unchanged. Choose finitely many turns so the positive and negative diagonal port coefficients each strictly dominate the sum of the absolute off-diagonal coefficients in that row. If D=Σc_i Q_i+D_Θ and |c_l| is maximal, the two l-ports have opposite signs: the l-term strictly dominates Σ_{i≠l}c_i Q_i, and D_Θ vanishes on U. Thus every relative periodic domain with nonzero Ξ-boundary has both signs after one fixed finite winding operation. Clearing denominators shows that this single operation applies to the integral lattice as well; no rational coefficient change is made in the Floer complex. [construct]

2.4 The winding is performed on all parallel strands of the same attaching family. Since τ_i has zero algebraic intersection with ξ_j for j≠i, the other strands return with their original net jump and can be kept on parallel tracks. Thus the family remains embedded and pairwise disjoint. Dual circles are constructed by cutting along the independent ξ-arcs and the protected meridional arc: the cut surface is connected, so join the two sides of each cut arc by a path in the complement, and close it through that arc. Move its crossing toward the boundary U without crossing Θ. This is the actual geometric dual construction used on the closure surfaces below. [construct]

2.5 **Positive fingers and good surface diagrams.** For a closed boundary component of a decomposing surface which is boundary-coherent in R(γ), choose a path from its exterior side to a suture. Push a short oriented boundary arc along that path and through the suture at a positive tangency. Attach the trace of this isotopy in a new boundary collar; collapsing the collar identifies the cut sutured manifold before and after the move. In the tangency chart the normal vector can become the positive surface normal, never its negative. Hence the outer vector-field condition is unchanged. For several parallel oriented curves use parallel tracks and the same positive tangency. For a homologically nonzero boundary curve, cut along it; both sides can be joined to sutures, and exactly one path orientation gives the positive tangency. Finitely many fingers make every boundary component meet both R₊ and R₋. This is a literal collar operation preserving the cut manifold and the outer set, not an arbitrary isotopy through negative tangencies. [construct]

2.6 For the resulting good surface, here is the relative Morse operation, without a fiber assumption. Remove narrow boundary fingers from S and round their ends so the remaining P has alternating crease arcs A,B ending on the true boundary. The removed strips on the A side run to R₊, and those on the B side to R₋. Set f₀=3/2 on P and prescribe its normal derivative so its gradient is never minus the oriented surface normal; in the strip collars extend the gradient to R₊ along A and to R₋ in negative time along B. Extend f₀ generically to the remaining compact manifold, fixing these collars and the boundary heights. Reorder its critical values by exchanging disjoint handle levels. The new middle surface is the old P surface with finitely many critical-handle tube feet. Clear those feet as follows. On each connected P component choose a rooted tree to A meeting every α arc, and push the α arcs along its corridors until each meets A. Do the same for β and B. For an α-belt tube foot connect it to B through the complement of the β arcs (every such component meets B), slide every crossed α disk over that belt, and move the B crease along the same corridor. This removes that foot. Use the color-reversed operation for β feet. All corridors are parallelized before the slides, so each attaching family remains disjoint. Repeat for the finite foot set; finally absorb the relative zero/one and two/three pairs by the rooted ball forests. The resulting balanced diagram carries the actual good S and its A/B creases. Cutting and doubling P literally cuts the prescribed gradient-thickened S. [construct]

2.7 To make it admissible while remaining adapted, choose a complete system of proper arcs in Σ\B relative to its true boundary, doubled into opposite parallel winding tracks. Every component of ∂(Σ\B) meets ∂Σ because B consists of arcs with boundary endpoints there. Intersection with these arcs detects every nonzero α-boundary combination in H₁(Σ\B); if a combination were zero there it would be zero in Σ, contradicting independence of the complete α disk system. Apply the port construction above in successive cut components, using a boundary zero region as U and making all Θ-only contributions zero on its ports. Every nonzero periodic domain has a nonzero α-boundary combination: if its α-boundary were zero, the balanced β-complement and its zero boundary coefficient would force the entire domain to be zero. Thus every nonzero periodic domain has both signs. All windings avoid B and carry P, so the result remains an actual good surface diagram. The completed permissible niceification then applies. [construct]

2.8 **All generators are outer for a separating balanced cut.** Suppose the connected good S separates M into balanced M₁ and M₂. In the actual cut/double diagram let P_A lie on the M₁ side and P_B on the M₂ side. Partition its attaching families into α¹,β¹ and α²,β². Balance gives |α^i|=|β^i|=d_i. Project back to the uncut surface. An α² circle misses P because its permitted copy P_A is on side one; a β¹ circle misses P because its permitted copy P_B is on side two. Their images cannot intersect outside P either, since the projection there is injective and the cut components are disjoint. Thus there are no α²β¹ intersection points. [construct]

2.9 An inner intersection, if present, has type α¹β². A generator is a perfect matching of α and β circles. The number of α¹β² matches must equal the number of α²β¹ matches, by subtracting the d₁ row and column counts. The latter is zero, so every generator avoids P. This is the exact cardinality argument; it does not claim that individual inner intersections are absent. It also does not use taut nonvanishing to assume that an outer generator exists: if no generator exists, both sides are the zero complex. [construct]

2.10 **Signed cut comparison with nonzero periodic domains.** Use the already constructed nice-disk exhaustion and literal local Fredholm conjugacies. They give a bijection of every differential disk with its cut lift. The remaining orientation question is not solved by asserting zero periodic domains. Choose the cut orientation character to be the pullback of the specified exterior character along the actual pushforward of periodic domains. The reference orientations are obtained by the same ordered real tangent caps on each copied intersection chart. For a loop of lifted rigid disks, the product of determinant-conjugacy ratios is the exterior character on its pushed domain minus the cut character on its original domain. It is zero by this pullback choice; the zero-domain sphere factor is complex oriented on both sides. A spanning forest of the finite generator graph now gives generator signs making every differential coefficient agree. Hence the full complex is integrally isomorphic to the cut complex with its specified induced class. This proves compatibility even if the cut has nonzero H₂. [construct]

2.11 For a separating open S, the homological pushforward is also concrete: H₂(S)=0, so the Mayer–Vietoris map H₂(M₁)⊕H₂(M₂)→H₂(M) is injective. The construction therefore retains all cut periodic classes; it has not quotiented out an invisible characteristic ambiguity. [construct]

2.12 **Actual tensor differential and the coefficient convention.** The cut diagram is a disjoint union of the two actual component diagrams. Its generators are pairs. A holomorphic disk splits into the two target components. Under a regular product choice, each nonconstant factor has positive index. An index-one disk consequently has precisely one nonconstant factor and a constant factor on the other side. Order the real determinant factors with side one first. Passing the odd differential operator past the orientation line of the first generator gives [construct]

2.13 ∂(x₁⊗x₂)=(∂₁x₁)⊗x₂+(−1)^|x₁| x₁⊗(∂₂x₂). [construct]

2.14 This supplies an actual integral chain isomorphism with the graded tensor product, including its Koszul sign. It yields Ni's homology tensor formula over every field. Over Z it instead yields the integral Künneth short exact sequence, with the Tor summands shifted by one parity; a plain homology tensor formula requires vanishing of those Tor groups. Finite free chain groups justify this directly by reducing each differential matrix to Smith normal form and decomposing into one-generator free blocks and two-generator multiplication-by-n blocks. Tensoring the blocks produces precisely the tensor and Tor terms. No torsion-freeness assumption is silently inserted. [construct]

2.15 For a horizontal surface, its class [R₊] gives the separating sides (the signed intersection of S with any closed loop is zero); its boundary and Euler equality make both cuts balanced. If S has several components, use the complementary-region adjacency graph and the same balanced matching counts, or apply the connected operation successively. In the usual two-piece horizontal case this is exactly Ni's horizontal chain operation. It uses neither a hierarchy nor a characteristic-product region. [construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Every smooth embedded torus in $S^3$ has a side whose closure is a parametrized smooth solid torus. If both sides are solid tori, there is an orientation-preserving smooth ambient isotopy taking this torus to a standard Clifford torus. Consequently every essential smooth circle on it is a torus knot or the unknot, through actual smooth ambient isotopies, not merely through an unspecified diffeomorphism of $S^3$.

If $T$ is an essential smooth torus in the interior of a chosen smooth knot exterior $E_K$, the side containing the knot tube is a parametrized solid torus $V$. It has a nontrivial smooth core knot $C$ and an orientation-preserving parameter $e:S^1\times D^2\to V$ identifying the positive meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $C$. The pattern $P=e^{-1}(K)$, with its pulled-back tube, gives the actual equality $K=P(C)$ and the actual exterior gluing along $T$. The pattern is not isotopic to the core in the solid torus. In particular this conclusion retains the actual essential companion torus and its meridian/longitude marking. No winding-nonzero assertion is imposed on a general satellite.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the smooth torus, or the essential torus and chosen knot tube, of the Statement.

[F1] Smooth two-sided geometric incompressibility is fundamental-group injectivity, and the smooth Loop construction gives a neat disk on a cut side. The three-sphere is simply connected. [[thm-smooth-loop-theorem-and-incompressibility-criterion-in-orientable-three-manifolds]], [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]]

[F2] Alexander duality separates an oriented closed torus in $S^3$ into two components. Smooth spheres have parametrized ball sides. Smooth disk windows can be standardized with their full parameters, and ball attachment/removal is supported in the specified receiving collar. [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]], [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F3] Essential smooth torus circles are primitive and normalize to affine circles by smooth isotopies. Compact-source embedding isotopies extend smoothly with prescribed compact support. The finite inverse-function argument gives injective common-width smooth coordinate neighborhoods. [[lem-choice-free-smooth-torus-curves-and-annulus-strips]], [[lem-choice-free-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-smooth-source]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]]

[F4] A smooth knot bounding a smooth disk is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot under countable choice. A preferred longitude is the unique primitive parallel of degree one on the knot and zero exterior homology. Exterior gluing has the actual connected-collar van Kampen pushout. [[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]], [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]], [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

## Proof

1.1 A smooth torus is two-sided: its orientation and that of $S^3$ give a nonzero smooth normal field and its short flow gives a product collar. Alexander duality in [F2] gives $\widetilde H_0(S^3\setminus T;\mathbb Z)\cong H^2(T;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$. The open complement is locally path-connected, so it has exactly two components. Each local collar side belongs to a single component, and each component meets such a side: otherwise it would also be closed in connected $S^3$. Connectedness of $T$ makes these side labels consistent. Their closures are therefore compact smooth manifolds with common boundary $T$. The map $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(S^3)$ is not injective, so [F1] gives an actual smooth compressing disk on one side, neat in that cut-side boundary. Its essential boundary on the torus is nonseparating. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

1.2 We need actual ambient control of a supplied solid-torus parameter. Let $e:S^1\times D^2\to S^3$ be any smooth embedding and let $c(\theta)=e(\theta,0)$. The paths $e(\theta,r(t)z)$, with $r(t)>0$ decreasing from one to a small $\epsilon$, are embedding isotopies fixing the core. Project the two transverse derivatives $e_{z_i}(\theta,0)$ onto the normal plane of $c$ in $S^3$ and apply Gram--Schmidt to get a smooth periodic normal frame $v_1,v_2$. Change one disk coordinate sign first if necessary. In that frame their normal derivative matrix $A(\theta)$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal. A concrete normal chart is $$\Phi(\theta,z)=\frac{c(\theta)+z_1v_1(\theta)+z_2v_2(\theta)}{\sqrt{1+|z|^2}}.$$ It is an embedding for one common small disk radius: its derivative at the zero section is invertible, finite inverse-function charts give local injectivity, and compact separation of distinct core parameters gives global injectivity. Write the shrunken map in these coordinates as $(a_\epsilon,n_\epsilon)$. The small periodic lift $a_\epsilon-\theta$ exists, and Taylor's formula gives $a_\epsilon-\theta=O(\epsilon)$ and $n_\epsilon/\epsilon-A(\theta)z=O(\epsilon)$ in $C^1$. Interpolate these two remainders linearly to zero. After rescaling the normal coordinate by $\epsilon$, every map is $C^1$ close to the fixed embedding $(\theta,z)\mapsto(\theta,A(\theta)z)$. This is quantitatively an embedding: on finitely many convex coordinate patches, derivative closeness to an invertible linear map gives a common lower bound on differences by integration along segments; pairs outside those patches are separated by compactness. Thus the interpolation is an embedding isotopy fixing the core. Finally interpolate $A$ to a small scalar identity through upper-triangular matrices with positive diagonal. The resulting image is a round normal tube of $c$. Apply [F3] to these actual compact-source isotopies, stationary at joins. They give an ambient isotopy fixing the core. If the initial solid torus is compactly contained in another ambient manifold, all supports can be chosen inside that manifold. No isotopy theorem for arbitrary three-ball diffeomorphisms is used. [F3, given, construct]

2.1 Cut the disk side at a thin neat disk neighborhood and round the supplied quadrants. Its new boundary is the single smooth sphere obtained by compressing $T$. The cut side is connected: every cut component has boundary, and the entire boundary is that one connected sphere. For the first assertion about components, every cut component meets either a disk face or the old boundary; a component meeting neither would already have been an open-and-closed component of the uncut connected side. The other side of $T$ lies outside the cut side. By smooth Schoenflies the compressed sphere has two ball sides. The cut-side interior is open and closed in one sphere-complement component, hence is that whole component, and its closure is its parametrized ball. Restore the disk neighborhood: this attaches one marked one-handle to that ball. This is an actual parametrized solid torus. To retain the parameters, standardize its two disjoint attaching disks in the ball boundary successively using [F2]'s full-window isotopies, the second supported away from the first; the complement is the corresponding smooth annulus. These boundary isotopies extend radially with an identity inner ball. Their collars match the given handle parameter. The result is the usual ball with one standard handle, equivalently the standard solid torus cut at one meridian disk. This proves the solid-torus-side assertion without recognizing an arbitrary manifold from its group. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Suppose now that $S^3=V_1\cup_TV_2$ with both $V_i$ parametrized solid tori. In the first parameter write the second meridian as $a\mu_1+b\lambda_1$. Boundary surjectivity onto $\pi_1(V_2)$ and van Kampen eliminate its core generator and give $\pi_1(S^3)\cong\mathbb Z/\langle b\rangle$. Hence $b=\pm1$. By [F3] a boundary isotopy carries that meridian to its affine slope. Inside $D^2\times S^1=V_1$, the formula $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r e^{ia\theta},e^{ib\theta})$ is an embedded annulus between this slope and the core; pull it back through the boundary collar isotopy to obtain the annulus with the ORIGINAL meridian rim. Glue its outer rim to the actual meridian disk in $V_2$ and round their neat seam. This is a smooth spanning disk for the core of $V_1$. By [F4] that core has an orientation-preserving smooth ambient unknot isotopy. Carry $V_1$ through it and apply step 1.2 to the transported parameter. For the standard round unknot the normal tube in the displayed $\Phi$ chart has Clifford-torus boundary; the frame rotation does not change its disk image. Thus the whole torus is carried to a standard Clifford torus by an actual ambient isotopy. Any essential circle carried with it has primitive class $(p,q)$ and normalizes there by [F3]. If both coordinates are nonzero, this is the defined coprime torus knot; if one vanishes, the other is $\pm1$ and the circle bounds a standard meridian disk on one side, hence is the unknot by [F4]. Full AC supplies the countable-choice uses. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Now assume $T\subset\operatorname{Int}E_K$ is essential. Its two sides in $S^3$ have the connected chosen tube $N(K)$ entirely on one side. A compressing disk from step 1.1 cannot be on the other side, for then it is a smooth compressing disk in $E_K$, contradicting essentiality. Therefore step 2.1 makes the side $V$ CONTAINING $N(K)$ a parametrized solid torus. Let $C$ be its smooth core. If $C$ were the unknot, its ambient unknot isotopy followed by the relative tube control of step 1.2 would identify $V$ with a standard unknotted tube. Its other side would be a solid torus, with a meridian disk lying entirely in $E_K$, again a compression of $T$. Thus $C$ is nontrivial. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct]

4.1 Choose the parameter $e_0:S^1\times D^2\to V$ orientation-preserving and orient $C$ by its core coordinate. Its meridian is the positive meridian of $C$. Its product longitude is a degree-one parallel, so it is $\lambda_C+k\mu_C$ for one integer $k$, by [F4]. Precompose with the explicit meridian twist $(\theta,z)\mapsto(\theta,e^{-ik\theta}z)$. This fixes the core and meridian and changes the longitude to exactly $\lambda_C$. Put $e$ equal to this corrected parameter, $P=e^{-1}(K)$ and $N(P)=e^{-1}(N(K))$. These are smooth marked pattern data inside the standard solid torus, and $e(P)=K$ literally. Their actual outer gluing to $E_C$ identifies $\mu_V,\lambda_V$ with $\mu_C,\lambda_C$, not merely with an unmarked peripheral basis. [F3, F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 If $P$ were isotopic to the core through smooth ambient isotopies of the solid torus, carry its chosen tube through that isotopy. Apply the compactly supported version of step 1.2 to make that tube a small round tube about the standard core, fixing the outer boundary. Its complement is then the explicit torus product between two concentric tubes. Pulling the product back gives a smooth product between the ACTUAL inner and outer pattern tori. Carry it by $e$: $T$ is boundary-parallel to $\partial E_K$, contradicting essentiality. Therefore $P$ is not isotopic to the core. All assertions preserve the given knot and torus through their specified parameters and actual isotopies; neither winding nonvanishing nor any atoroidal hyperbolization has been assumed. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 4.1, construct] ∎

title: Balanced taut sutured manifolds admit finite good hierarchies

      url: https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Lectures-3-mfld-topology_Jaco.pdf

## Statement

Let $(M,\gamma)$ be a compact orientable finite PL balanced taut sutured three-manifold. There is a finite sequence of balanced taut sutured decompositions terminating in product balls. Each decomposing surface may be chosen open, with every boundary component meeting both signed boundary regions after positive boundary fingers; in each signed boundary component its closed intersection curves are parallel coherently oriented boundary-coherent curves. Product disk cuts may be interspersed. No closed cut is required.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Balanced, taut and product use the conventions of [[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region]].

[F2] The finite sequential length and its strict decrease for essential incompressible boundary-incompressible nondisk cuts are supplied by [[lem-essential-proper-haken-cuts-have-finite-sequential-length]].

## Proof

**Given:** A balanced taut finite PL sutured manifold in the convention F1, and the precise sequential rank supplied by F2. All surgeries and choices in the proof concern finite complexes and nonnegative integer minima.

### Norm construction needed for the taut cut

1.1 For a properly embedded oriented surface $T$ and a finite collection $\delta$ of auxiliary properly embedded arcs, define $$x_\delta(T)=\sum_{T_i}\max\{0,|T_i\cap\delta|-\chi(T_i)\}.$$ [given, construct]

1.2 The empty-arc version is the ordinary Thurston complexity. For a relative homology class $a$, minimize this nonnegative integer over representatives. The minimum exists whenever the class has a representative. Compression and the removal of intersection pairs of opposite sign never increase the value: a compression raises Euler characteristic by two, and tubing opposite intersections together removes two marked intersections at exactly that Euler cost. Thus a minimum can be chosen incompressible and with coherent intersections on each auxiliary arc. [step 1.1, construct]

1.3 The homogeneity needed here has a direct geometric proof. If an embedded oriented $T$ represents $na$, color the components of its complement by $\mathbb Z/n$, assigning a color by intersection number of a path with $T$. This is well-defined because every closed test loop has intersection divisible by $n$. For relative homology use also paths with endpoints on the complementary boundary; their colors are normalized to zero there, since the relative dual class of $T$ is divisible by $n$. Crossing a positive normal increases the color by one. Each connected component of $T$ has two fixed adjacent colors, so partition the whole components into $T_0,\ldots,T_{n-1}$ according to the transition $j\to j+1$. [step 1.2, construct]

1.4 Every closed or relative test path crosses each such transition with the same algebraic total: its sequence of colors is a walk on the cyclic color graph, and the difference of two transition counts is its net occupancy change at a vertex, which is zero. Its total intersection with $T$ is consequently $n$ times its intersection with each $T_j$. Relative Poincaré duality gives $[T_j]=a$. The norm adds over this partition of whole components, so $x_\delta(T)\ge n x_\delta(a)$. Conversely $n$ parallel minimizing representatives give the opposite inequality. Hence $x_\delta(na)=n x_\delta(a)$. [step 1.3, construct]

1.5 For subadditivity, put two minimizing representatives in general position. Eliminate inessential intersection circles and arcs by innermost/outermost compression and boundary surgery. The remaining intersections are essential in both surfaces. Their oriented double-curve sum preserves total Euler characteristic and marked intersection count. None of its zero-complexity components introduces a negative correction to the inequality. Thus $x_\delta(a+b)\le x_\delta(a)+x_\delta(b)$. Integer homogeneity and this inequality give convexity on rational classes; a bound on a homology basis gives the continuous extension if desired. [step 1.4, construct]

1.6 For fixed integral classes $a,b$, the integers $$d_n=x_\delta(a+(n+1)b)-x_\delta(a+nb)$$ [step 1.5, construct]

1.7 are nondecreasing by convexity and at most $x_\delta(b)$ by subadditivity. They are therefore eventually constant. Homogeneity shows that their eventual value is $x_\delta(b)$, by dividing $x_\delta(a+nb)$ by $n$ and using the two triangle bounds with $\pm a$. Consequently for some $m$, $$x_\delta(a+(m+k)b)=x_\delta(a+mb)+k x_\delta(b),\qquad k\ge0.$$ [step 1.6, construct]

1.8 This proves the eventual linearity used to choose the cut; it is not imported as an unexplained property of a named norm. [step 1.7, construct]

### Constructing a taut decomposing surface with prescribed boundary

1.9 Let $(M,\gamma)$ be taut, and let $y\ne0$ in $H_2(M,\partial M)$. Choose an oriented boundary representative $C$ of $\partial y$, in the complement of small collars of the boundary sutures. Let $R$ be the signed boundary surfaces, pushed slightly into $M$. Put $N=\nu(\partial R\cup C)$ in $\partial M$ and choose disjoint arcs $\delta$ in $N$ whose complement retracts to the individual boundary circles of $R$ and the closed components of $C$. Push those arcs slightly into $M$. [step 1.8, construct]

1.10 This choice has two concrete consequences. A representative of $[R]$ minimizing the marked norm can be made disjoint from $\delta$ and then has boundary exactly $\partial R$, by adding boundary annuli. Tautness of $R$ therefore shows that $R$ also minimizes the marked norm in $H_2(M,N)$. Also $R$ is incompressible relative to $N\setminus\delta$: an essential boundary compression would lower the marked norm except for an annulus; that annulus would connect two boundary circles in a single component of $N\setminus\delta$, excluded by construction. A disk exception cannot have an essential compressing arc. [step 1.9, construct]

1.11 Lift $y$ to $H_2(M,N)$ and choose $z=y+m[R]$ in the eventual linear range just proved. Choose a marked-norm-minimizing representative $S$. Oppositely oriented intersection circles in $R$ can be removed by cutting and regluing along their annulus. Innermost-circle and outermost-arc surgeries make all intersections with $R$ essential in both surfaces. Compress further away from $R$ to make $S$ incompressible; incompressibility of $R$ and irreducibility of $M$ allow those compressions without reintroducing inessential intersections. Its boundary outside $\nu\partial R$ is exactly $C$. [step 1.10, construct]

1.12 For any subcollection $R'$ of parallel copies of the components of $R$, choose a large parallel multiple $kR$ containing it. The inequalities $$x_\delta(z)+k x_\delta(R) =x_\delta(z+kR) \le x_\delta(z+R')+x_\delta(kR-R') \le x_\delta(z)+x_\delta(R')+x_\delta(kR-R')$$ [step 1.11, construct]

1.13 have equal endpoints, since subcollections of a taut surface minimize their classes. Thus equality holds throughout. Essential double-curve summing gives an actual minimizing representative $S\mathbin{\#}R'$. [step 1.12, construct]

1.14 Its incompressibility needs the zero-norm case as well as the numerical equality. A compressible component of a minimizing sum must have zero norm. A disk or punctured sphere then compresses a piece of $S$ or $R'$, impossible. A compressible annulus contradicts essentiality of its boundary intersection circles. A compressible torus bounds a solid torus by irreducibility. An intersecting annular piece of $R'$ inside that solid torus has two oppositely oriented boundary circles in $R'$, exactly the antiparallel pair already eliminated. A torus lying wholly in one input is excluded by its incompressibility. These exhaust the zero-norm possibilities. Hence the sums are taut, not merely numerically minimizing. [step 1.13, construct]

1.15 Removing the auxiliary arcs does not destroy tautness: a candidate with lower unmarked norm can be made to have the same prescribed boundary, so its extra marked intersections are the same boundary contribution; compressing it cannot increase that contribution. It would then contradict the marked minimum. This is the only use of those arcs, which are not part of the eventual sutured manifold. [step 1.14, construct]

1.16 Cap opposite boundary curves in the annular suture collars by annuli, and discard closed separating components. Because $R$ is boundary-parallel, its class vanishes in $H_2(M,\partial M)$; thus the resulting surface still represents $y$. The new signed boundaries of the cut manifold are the actual oriented sums $R_+\mathbin{\#}S$ and $R_-\mathbin{\#}S$. They are taut by the construction. A reducing sphere in the cut manifold bounds a ball in $M$; incompressibility removes its intersections with $S$, so its ball stays in the cut manifold. This proves tautness after cutting. [step 1.15, construct]

### Positive boundary fingers

1.17 Write an annular suture as $[-1,1]\times S^1$ and its oriented core as $\{0\}\times S^1$. A positive tangency is one at which the oriented boundary curve of the decomposing surface and the oriented suture have the same tangent direction. In a small oriented boundary chart take the core to be $y=0$, directed by $\partial_x$, and the moving boundary arc to be $y=x^2-t$, also directed by increasing $x$. Passing through $t=0$ creates the required pair of transverse intersections with the core. [step 1.16, construct]

1.18 Keep track of the actual surface during this move by attaching the collar $\partial M\times[0,1]$ and adding the trace annulus of its moving boundary. The trace annulus has its old boundary on level zero and its moved boundary on level one; glue its old boundary to the original surface. Cutting the collar along this annulus gives the old cut manifold with an attached boundary collar. At the tangency the two new corners bound a three-ball whose incoming and outgoing face are disks; sliding one disk across that ball removes the two corners. Their suture orientations agree precisely for the positive tangency. Thus the sutured cut manifold is unchanged up to diffeomorphism. A negative tangency has the opposite suture attachment and is not included in this assertion. [step 1.17, construct]

1.19 Here is a terminating normalization for a boundary-coherent family. First move any closed curves lying in an annular suture into its adjacent negative boundary region, with the normal of the decomposing surface pointing out of the manifold. An arc transverse to all those parallel curves, continued across the suture to the positive region, gives simultaneous positive fingers because the curves have the same orientation. [step 1.18, construct]

1.20 Next let $C_1,\ldots,C_k$ be the parallel oriented closed intersection curves in a component $V$ of the positive or negative boundary. A short transverse arc crosses each once. If their homology class in $H_1(V)$ is nonzero, the two sides of this family can be connected to the sutures without crossing the family: the family does not cut off a compact subsurface away from the boundary. Continue the transverse arc on its two sides to obtain the finger path. Exactly one orientation of that path gives positive tangencies for every curve, since all their orientations agree. [step 1.19, construct]

1.21 If their homology class is zero, boundary coherence says that each is the oriented boundary of the compact side it cuts off. Continue the transverse arc from its exterior side to a suture. This gives a one-ended finger path. The boundary orientation of that compact side and the boundary orientation of $V$ again give positive tangencies. No assertion for oppositely oriented boundaries of compact sides is needed. [step 1.20, construct]

1.22 Choose the continuation arcs successively in the complement of the other boundary arcs. At each stage use an outermost parallel family. The components already meeting both signed boundary regions need not be moved. Each operation reduces the number of boundary components lying wholly in one signed region; no new wholly contained component is created. Hence finitely many moves give a good decomposing surface: every component of its boundary meets both signed regions. The actual cut sutured manifold is preserved by the collar-and-ball construction at every move. This establishes the normalization step rather than treating boundary coherence as an analytic nonvanishing theorem. [step 1.21, construct]

1.23  ## Keeping the cuts open and boundary coherent [step 1.22, construct]

1.24 For the balanced application, no closed boundary component is allowed to lose all sutures. If a nonterminal component has boundary of positive genus, the kernel of $H_1(\partial M;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(M;\mathbb Q)$ is a Lagrangian of half the boundary rank, by the long exact sequence and intersection duality. Choose $y$ with nonzero $\partial y$ in this kernel. Thus a representative has a proper component with nonzero relative class. [step 1.23, construct]

1.25 The boundary representative can be chosen with the needed parallel-curve condition on each signed region $V$. Represent its relative class by disjoint arcs and curves. If there is an arc, band each closed curve to an arc along a path in their complement; the band replaces the pair by a single arc and preserves the relative class. Repeat until no closed curve remains. If there are no arcs, the class modulo boundary circles is an element of the symplectic integral homology of $V$. Write it as a positive multiple of a primitive vector. Euclidean elementary changes of a handle basis, realized by twists and band sums, carry that primitive vector to one handle core. Pulling that core back gives a nonseparating simple closed curve; take the indicated number of oriented parallel copies. Boundary-parallel homology terms can be moved into the annular sutures. Thus the closed curves in $V$ may be chosen parallel, coherently oriented and nonseparating. The taut-cut construction above preserves this chosen boundary outside the suture collars. [step 1.24, construct]

1.26 The strong norm equalities also allow one to keep a proper component rather than all components of $S$. Write $S=S_0\sqcup T$. Each is minimizing, since they are component subcollections. The two triangle inequalities for $[S_0]+[R']+[T]$, together with equality for $S+R'$, force equality for $S_0+R'$. The essential-intersection and zero-norm incompressibility argument restricts to that subcollection. Thus its two signed boundary sums remain taut. Choose a proper $S_0$ whose boundary class is nonzero. It is connected, open, and has nonzero relative class. The positive boundary fingers just constructed make it good without changing the cut sutured manifold. [step 1.25, construct]

1.27 Cutting an open good surface preserves balance: every boundary circle alternates the signed boundary regions when passing through sutures. The numbers of boundary arcs glued into $R_+$ and $R_-$ are equal. Both new signed surfaces acquire the same $\chi(S_0)$ contribution and the same arc subtraction, so their Euler characteristics remain equal. Every new boundary component has an old or a new annular suture, because every side of the cut surface reaches its nonempty boundary. Closed pieces are not produced. This identifies the version needed by the sutured instanton consumer, rather than silently treating a closed cut as balanced. [step 1.26, construct]

### The finite complexity decrease, at empty marking

1.28 A boundary-compressing disk $D$ has index $I(D)=v(D)-2$, where $v(D)$ counts its passages through annular sutures. Tautness excludes negative-index essential disks. Index-zero disks are exactly product disks and can first be eliminated, preserving tautness by the literal signed-boundary cut-and-reglue argument. [step 1.27, construct]

1.29 Choose a maximal compression system $D_i$ cutting $M$ into boundary-irreducible pieces $M_k$, closed-surface products $P_\mu$, and handlebodies. Choose further meridian disks $E_j$ cutting each handlebody into balls meeting at most three disk faces. Write $d_k$ for the number of $D_i$ faces on $M_k$, and $d'_\mu$ for the number on $P_\mu$. The exact ordered complexity is $$\left(\sum_k\ell(M_k),\ \sum_i I(D_i)^2, \ \sum_k d_k,\ m+\sum_\mu(d'_\mu)^2, \ \{I(D_i)>0\}\cup\{I(E_j)>0\}\right).$$ [step 1.28, construct]

1.30 The last entry is a descending finite multiset, ordered lexicographically. Replace positive entries by positive proper parts only decreases it. For a precise well-order, encode a multiset by $\sum_n a_n\omega^n$, with coefficient $a_n$ its multiplicity. The first four entries are nonnegative integers. Minimize this tuple over disk systems, and then minimize it after eliminating product disks; this is the reduced complexity. [step 1.29, construct]

1.31 Here $\ell(M_k)$ is the finite essential-Haken-length rank of F2, which strictly decreases on an essential boundary-incompressible nondisk cut. Its precise scope matches case(1) below; merely incompressible cuts are not admitted to that rank. [step 1.30, construct]

1.32 Put a connected taut nonzero cut surface in minimal position with these disks. Innermost-circle isotopy removes intersection circles. At an outermost arc, a nonpositive-index disk performs a boundary compression or a product-disk cut after the surface cut; this preserves the resulting reduced complexity and tautness. Repeating leaves only positive outermost pieces. Under a disk cut the sum of the indices of all resulting disks equals its original index: the two new endpoints increase the total suture-passage count by two and the number of disks by one. [step 1.31, construct]

1.33 There are six exhaustive locations for the remaining surface. (1) An essential piece in $M_k$ strictly lowers $\ell(M_k)$, the first coordinate. (2) Intersection with some $D_i$ splits its positive index into at least two positive parts, so the sum of squares strictly drops. (3) A surface parallel into the boundary of $M_k$ either is parallel into the boundary of all of $M$, or cuts off at least one $D_i$ face and lowers $\sum d_k$. (4) In a product piece $P_\mu$, an essential cut partitions its $D_i$ faces between two nonempty pieces: a new product piece adds one, while $a^2+b^2\le(a+b)^2-2$ offsets that increase and strictly lowers the fourth coordinate. A proper boundary cut instead removes faces and also lowers it. (5) In a handlebody, intersection with $E_j$ splits its positive index into proper positive indices and decreases the final multiset. To retain ball pieces with at most three disk faces, take parallel levels of $E_j$ separating successive saddle heights of the surface; each complementary piece is a ball with at most three faces. (6) If the surface misses all those disks, it is parallel to one of them; remove that disk from the system and decrease the last multiset. The only exceptional nondecreasing case is a surface parallel into $\partial M$, whose relative class is zero and which our chosen cut excludes. [step 1.32, construct]

1.34 Thus the chosen nonzero component is replaced by finitely many components of strictly lower reduced complexity. Other components can be left in a work queue. The finite-tree descending-rank argument terminates: an infinite finitely branching cut tree would have an infinite branch, contradicting the well-order. Repeat the taut-cut construction only when $H_2(M,\partial M)\ne0$. [step 1.33, construct]

1.35 At termination, Poincaré–Lefschetz duality gives $b_1(M)=0$. The half-lives/half-dies boundary sequence then gives boundary genus zero. Irreducibility forces a connected component with spherical boundary to be a ball: push one boundary sphere slightly into its interior; the ball it bounds leaves only its boundary collar on the other side. Multiple boundary spheres would contradict that same assertion. On a ball, incompressible signed boundary regions must be disks, and their connected sutured partition has exactly one annular suture; any additional suture would enclose an annular signed region with a compressing disk. Thus each terminal component is a product disk times an interval. This supplies the actual terminal product topology at empty marking. [step 1.34, construct] ∎
